Multi-task entries on this board use extra supervision (contact prediction, secondary structure) that is listed in the 'external data' column; a comparison must respect what each entry was allowed to use.
The page hosts several boards with different metrics; quoting a solubility accuracy against the fold-classification bar is a category error.
Leaderboards hosted on a project site can go stale, so the novelty check must search the literature for higher published numbers on the same split before any claim.
targets.statement: PEER (Minghao Xu and co-authors, TorchProtein/TorchDrug) maintains public leaderboards for protein-sequence tasks at torchprotein.ai/benchmark, with fixed splits, published dataset statistics and per-entry parameter counts. The hardest board is fold classification: entire SCOP 1.75 superfamilies are held out, so the test proteins have similar structures but dissimilar sequences to anything in training, and the model must name one of 1195 folding topologies. The top listed accuracy is 32.10% (+/- 0.72) for a multi-task ESM-1b with contact prediction, then 29.95% for frozen ESM-1b; a plain CNN and LSTM are far lower. Two thirds of the test set is still misclassified, with 12,312 training and 718 test proteins, which is small enough to train on a laptop CPU in hours with a modest model on top of cached embeddings. Related boards on the same page are also unsaturated (solubility 70.63%, subcellular localization 79.82%).
targets.success_criterion: Predicted fold labels for every protein in the PEER fold-classification test split, from a model trained only on the task's designated training set (plus publicly declared pretraining corpora that contain no SCOP 1.75 superfamily labels for the test superfamilies), whose test accuracy computed by the skeptic with the task's standard accuracy definition is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the top accuracy listed on https://torchprotein.ai/benchmark for fold classification (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 1.5 percentage points, reported as mean and standard deviation over at least three seeds, and higher than any later published value found by the novelty check.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic obtains the PEER fold-classification split through the TorchProtein data loaders (public download, no registration), checks the prediction file covers each test protein exactly once, computes accuracy, reruns the attacker's training script from the released seed to reproduce the number within its stated standard deviation, and checks that no test superfamily appears in training. An hour or two.

angles: Frozen small ESM-2 embeddings per protein, then a symmetric pair model (sum and elementwise product of embeddings) with strong regularisation; most of the gain may come from good per-protein features, not the pair architecture.

Cross-domain import (recommender systems): factorisation machines / two-tower models trained with degree-debiased negative sampling, exactly the setting of cold-start users and items, which is what disjoint proteins are.
Cross-domain import (structural biology): predicted interface propensity per residue (from a small structure-aware model or sequence-only interface predictors) aggregated into a pair score.
Domain-domain interaction priors: map both proteins to Pfam domains and score pairs by domain co-occurrence statistics computed from the TRAINING split only.
Co-evolution is unavailable for most human pairs, but paralog-based 'interolog' transfer within the training split can still carry signal; test it honestly under the gold-standard split.
targets.name: Leakage-free protein-protein interaction prediction: beat the best published AUPR on the Bernett gold-standard human dataset

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best published AUROC (0.703 as of 2026-10-13) by >= 0.02 with a CPU-trainable model, even if AUPRC does not clear its bar.

A degree- and similarity-controlled ablation on the gold standard showing which part of the prediction comes from genuine pair-specific signal (e.g. permuting partners within degree bins), checkable from released code.

pitfalls: The whole point of the dataset is to remove leakage: any external PPI database, or a pretrained model fine-tuned on PPIs that include test proteins, re-introduces it. Pretrained protein language models trained on sequences alone are allowed; PPI-supervised checkpoints are not.
Node-degree shortcuts: the dataset balances degrees, but a model can still exploit residual degree signal; report a degree-only baseline.
Accuracy depends on a threshold; claim on AUPR (threshold-free) and report the others for context.

The published record is assembled from papers rather than a live leaderboard, and DCAPPI's AUPRC exceeds its AUROC, which hints at different evaluation details; the skeptic must recompute on the official test files and the NOVELTY skeptic must search for newer results on this exact split.

C3PI's own paper reports 0.977 AUROC / 0.878 AUPRC on a DIFFERENT dataset (its Table 3); quoting that as the gold-standard bar would make the target look saturated when it is not. Only values on the Bernett gold-standard split count.
targets.statement: Bernett, Blumenthal and List (Briefings in Bioinformatics 2024) showed that sequence-based PPI predictors that report 95-99% accuracy learn mostly sequence similarity and node degree, and that on a carefully de-leaked human split their performance falls to near random. They released a gold-standard dataset (figshare 21591618, version 4: Intra0/1/2 positive and negative pair files plus a SwissProt FASTA) with disjoint, similarity-minimised train/validation/test proteins and balanced degrees. On its test split, the methods Bernett et al. evaluated score AUROC 0.50-0.59 (Topsy-Turvy best). Hosseini, Golding and Ilie (C3PI, Briefings in Bioinformatics 2025) reached AUROC 0.703 / AUPRC 0.695, TUnA reports AUROC 0.700 / AUPRC 0.690, and Lu, Li, Tian, Nan et al. (DCAPPI, Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal 2026, Table 5) report AUROC 0.702 / AUPRC 0.743. Everything sits around 0.70 AUROC, far from the 0.95+ seen on leaky benchmarks. Laptop-scale protein language model embeddings (ESM-2 8M-150M on CPU) are enough to compete.
targets.success_criterion: A score for every pair in the gold-standard test files (Intra2 positives and negatives, figshare 21591618 v4), produced by a model trained only on Intra1 (and validated on Intra0), whose AUPR recomputed by the skeptic with scikit-learn's average_precision_score is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best published AUPRC on this split (Table 5 of the DCAPPI paper at the Europe PMC full-text URL, re-fetched live immediately before claiming, plus any newer work found by the NOVELTY check) by at least 0.02, AND whose AUROC is strictly higher than the best published AUROC, with bootstrap 95% intervals over test pairs that exclude the published bests. No external PPI database (STRING, BioGRID, IntAct, HuRI) may be used.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the gold-standard files through the figshare v2 API (https://api.figshare.com/v2/articles/21591618, which lists Intra0/1/2_pos_rr.txt, Intra0/1/2_neg_rr.txt and the SwissProt FASTA with direct ndownloader.figshare.com links; the figshare web page answers a plain GET with an empty 202), checks the score file covers each test pair exactly once, computes AUPR/AUROC with scikit-learn, bootstraps over pairs, and audits the code for any read of the test files during training and any external interaction database. Minutes.

angles: Training sets here are hundreds to thousands of variants of one protein, so a one-hot or substitution-matrix ridge regression is a strong baseline; establish it first and only then ask whether an embedding model beats it.

Cross-domain import (chemometrics): several properties are measured per variant; partial least squares on the joint response borrows strength across correlated assays, which single-task models cannot.

Cross-domain import (quantitative genetics): treat the measurements as a trait with additive effects plus epistasis and fit a kinship-style model on sequence similarity, which handles few examples and many positions.
Zero-shot scores from a protein language model can serve as a prior for the regression rather than a competitor, which is where the supervised and zero-shot tracks meet.
Beta-glucosidase B has the smallest training set; test explicitly whether the collapse there is sample size by subsampling the larger events to the same size.
targets.name: Protein Engineering Tournament pilot (supervised track): beat the best team Spearman on a released enzyme property

partial_wins.statement: beta-glucosidase B: average Spearman above 0.30 (best team value 0.078 as of 2026-10-15) with the frozen procedure, on an event where both participating teams were near or below zero.
One frozen procedure that beats the best team value on two of the four events at once, which no single team achieved.

A per-property breakdown (the events score several measurements each) showing which property drives the average, plus a reproducible demonstration of whether small training sets or property noise set the ceiling.

pitfalls: A 'test (with values).csv' file sits next to test.csv in the repository; reading it during training or model selection is test-label peeking and voids the claim.
Some of the pilot's measurements appear in public enzyme databases and in protein language model training corpora; declare pretrained weights and check for the exact variants.
The boards average Spearman across several property columns; quoting a single property's correlation against the board value is not the same quantity.
Sample sizes are small (tens to hundreds of test rows), so Spearman is noisy; hence the 0.05 margin and bootstrap requirement.
A better prediction on a pilot dataset is not a validated enzyme improvement, and the in-vitro track of the tournament showed how often computational picks fail expression and stability screens.
targets.statement: The pilot Protein Engineering Tournament (Chase Armer, Hassan Kane, Dana Cortade, Hanna Redestig, David Estell, Adil Yusuf, Nathan Rollins, Alex Spinner, Debora Marks, T. J. Brunette, Peter Kelly, Erika DeBenedictis; Proteins 2025, bioRxiv 2024.08.12.606135) released every dataset, every team submission and the scoring notebooks under CC BY at github.com/the-protein-engineering-tournament/pet-pilot-2023. In the supervised in-silico track, teams got train.csv and predicted held-out property values; the published board (doc/supervised-board.csv) shows average Spearman of 0.822 (nimbus) on alpha-amylase, 0.697 (exazyme) on imine reductase, 0.613 (tum-rostlab) on alkaline phosphatase PafA, and just 0.078 (exazyme) on beta-glucosidase B, where the other team scored -0.300. Test files with values are in the repository, so anyone can train on train.csv and score honestly. Two of the four events are barely above chance, which is where the headroom is. These are enzyme engineering targets of the kind used for biocatalysis and therapeutic protein optimisation.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for every row of a supervised-track event's test file, from a model trained only on that event's train.csv (and publicly declared pretrained weights whose training data do not contain the event's measured values), whose average Spearman across the event's property columns, recomputed by the skeptic with the repository's evaluation.ipynb, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best team value for that event in doc/supervised-board.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.05, with the same frozen procedure run on all four supervised events and every result reported, and with a bootstrap 95% interval over test rows excluding the previous best.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the repository (a few hundred megabytes), checks the prediction file covers each test row exactly once, runs the event's scoring cells from evaluation.ipynb, confirms from the training script that only train.csv was read, and compares with doc/supervised-board.csv. Minutes.

angles: Negative Spearman for several teams suggests sign and convention errors rather than no signal; fix the convention first, using an unrelated public deep mutational scan to choose it, and see how much of the gap closes.

Cross-domain import (ensemble forecasting): average the ranks of several independent weak predictors (alignment conservation, a small language model, a biophysical stability estimate) rather than trusting one model, which is standard practice where individual skill is low.
Cross-domain import (structural engineering): score mutations by predicted change in packing and electrostatics around the catalytic residues, which is mechanistic and needs no training data.

These are industrial enzymes with large natural families; build a family alignment from public sequence databases and use covariation, which is often stronger than a general-purpose model for one protein.
The xylanase event is classification rather than correlation; calibrating a continuous score into classes without peeking at labels is itself the hard part and can be done on an unrelated assay.
targets.name: Protein Engineering Tournament pilot (zero-shot track): beat the best team score on an unseen enzyme

partial_wins.statement: Aminotransferase: average Spearman above 0.30 (best team value 0.163 as of 2026-10-15) with a frozen zero-shot method, on an event where two of four teams scored at or below zero.
One frozen method that is above zero on all three events and beats the best team on at least one, which no participant achieved.

A reproducible comparison of scoring conventions for multi-mutant variants (masked marginals, wild-type marginals, whole-sequence likelihood) on these events, showing how much of the published spread between teams is convention rather than model.

pitfalls: Using the supervised track's training data for the same or a homologous enzyme makes the method not zero-shot; the tracks share organisms and must be kept separate.
Fitting the sign of the correlation on the event's own values is the most common invisible leak here and would explain large apparent gains.
The three events use two different metrics; a claim must use the metric the board uses for that event.
Test sets are small (roughly a hundred to a few thousand variants), so differences below 0.05 Spearman are not meaningful.
Winning a ranking event does not mean the top-ranked designs work: in the tournament's in-vitro round, many submitted designs failed expression or stability screens.
targets.statement: In the zero-shot in-silico track of the pilot Protein Engineering Tournament (Armer, Kane, Cortade, Redestig, Estell, Yusuf, Rollins, Spinner, Marks, Brunette, Kelly, DeBenedictis; Proteins 2025), teams received only sequences and had to rank variants of three enzymes with no training data. The published board (doc/zero-shot-board.csv) shows how hard this is: on alpha-amylase the best average Spearman is 0.401 (marks-lab) and one team is at -0.261; on aminotransferase the best is 0.163 (marks-lab) with another team at -0.283; on the xylanase classification event the best weighted F1 is 0.641 with accuracy 0.567 (marks-lab), against five submissions. Evaluation data with measured values and the scoring notebook are public in the repository, so the bar is reproducible offline. Ranking variants of an enzyme nobody has assayed is the core capability claimed for protein language models, and on this release they are close to useless on two of three events.
targets.success_criterion: Scores for every variant in a zero-shot event's evaluation file, produced by a method that reads none of that event's measured values at any stage (no threshold, sign or hyperparameter fitted on them), whose average Spearman (or weighted F1 and accuracy for the xylanase event), recomputed by the skeptic with the repository's evaluation.ipynb, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best team value for that event in doc/zero-shot-board.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.05, with the same frozen method applied to all three zero-shot events and all results reported.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the repository, checks the score file covers every evaluation row, runs the event's cells in in_silico_zero-shot/evaluation.ipynb, confirms from the code that the measured-value columns were never read, and compares with doc/zero-shot-board.csv. Minutes.

angles: Rank-average ensemble of precomputed ProteinGym model scores (released in the repo) plus ESM-2 650M masked-marginals, with ensemble weights fixed from OTHER assays only.
Structure-aware thermodynamic proxy: ESM-IF / ProteinMPNN log-likelihoods on the AlphaFold DB structure for stability assays.
Evolutionary model: EVmutation/Potts model trained on a fresh jackhmmer MSA with tuned reweighting, combined with site-conservation priors.

Cross-domain import (recommender systems): low-rank matrix factorisation across assays x models to learn which model families transfer to which protein families, then pick per-assay without using its labels.
Cross-domain import (econometrics/forecast combination): Bates-Granger optimal forecast combination with shrinkage, fit leave-one-assay-out.
Cross-domain import (NLP calibration): temperature/position-specific calibration of PLM logits using unlabeled mutational spectra (entropy normalization per site).
targets.name: ProteinGym zero-shot substitutions: beat every listed model's Spearman on a single DMS assay

partial_wins.statement: A frozen laptop-runnable method (<= 650M params) whose average Spearman over all Stability assays exceeds the 10th-ranked model's Stability column in the Summary CSV.
Beat the row max on a Low_MSA_depth assay with a method using no MSA.

pitfalls: Label leakage: any tuning, ensembling weight or model selection that touches the target assay's DMS_score is supervised, not zero-shot. Freeze before scoring.
Cherry-picking: beating the row max on one of 217 assays by chance is likely for a noisy small assay; require the frozen method be reported on the whole category and pre-registered.
Several assay rows have very few mutants; Spearman bootstrap SE can exceed the margin. Require margin > bootstrap SE.
Disease-relevant assays (human disease genes, viral proteins) belong to another lane; restrict to non-disease assays.
The CSVs on main changed in Jan/Mar 2026; always compare to the live file, not a cached copy.
targets.statement: ProteinGym (OATML-Markslab) publishes, for 217 deep-mutational-scanning assays, the Spearman correlation of every benchmarked zero-shot fitness predictor (~100 models) in DMS_substitutions_Spearman_DMS_level.csv; the overall leaders (AIDO Protein-RAG 16B, VenusREM, ~0.518 average) are listed in the Summary CSV. Restricted to non-disease assays (stability, activity, binding, expression of non-pathogen proteins). Produce zero-shot scores (no use of the assay's own labels) that achieve a Spearman strictly higher than the maximum over all listed models for at least one assay.
targets.success_criterion: For one non-disease assay in the live DMS-level CSV at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym/main/benchmarks/DMS_zero_shot/substitutions/Spearman/DMS_substitutions_Spearman_DMS_level.csv (re-fetched immediately before claiming), a saved score file (mutant, score) produced by a frozen, pre-registered method whose code never reads the assay's DMS_score column, such that ProteinGym's own Spearman routine yields a value strictly greater than the row maximum over all listed models; the method's hyperparameters must be fixed before scoring the target assay (pre-registration hash), and the same method must be run on all assays in the same function category with results reported.
targets.verification_method: Download the assay CSV from the ProteinGym data release, run the official Spearman computation on the submitted score file, compare to the live DMS-level row max; skeptic re-runs the frozen method on the assay from the pre-registered commit to reproduce the score file byte-for-byte (or within float tolerance). Under an hour per assay for small models.

angles: The metric is signed, so a model that ranks variants in the wrong direction scores below zero; calibrate direction per category on a held-out category rather than per assay, which would peek at labels.

Thermodynamics instead of language models: score each variant by the change in ensemble free energy or base-pair probability of the catalytic core under a stock folding package, which is almost free on a CPU and is a real mechanism for ribozyme cleavage.

Cross-domain import (evolutionary biology): build a covariation model from the released alignments and score variants by coupling terms, the approach that works for proteins in deep mutational scanning, which no listed RNA model does explicitly.

Cross-domain import (psychometrics): with 26 ribozyme assays and few tRNA and aptamer assays, the macro average is dominated by small, high-variance categories; treat it as a reliability problem and build an ensemble whose weights are fitted on category-level cross-validation across assays, never on variant labels.

Most variants here carry several mutations at once, so scoring conventions for multi-mutants (masked-marginal sums versus whole-sequence likelihood) change results more than model size; search that convention space explicitly on a held-out category.
targets.name: RNAGym ncRNA fitness: beat the top signed-Spearman macro score on the live zero-shot leaderboard

partial_wins.statement: Ribozyme category alone: mean signed Spearman over the 26 ribozyme assays above the best listed ribozyme column value (0.1343 for RNA-ERNIE as of 2026-10-15) by at least 0.02, with the same frozen method run on all 31 assays.

A laptop-runnable baseline (thermodynamic folding energy change, covariation from the released alignments, or a model under 200M parameters) that beats every listed model of 1B parameters or more on at least one category, showing the leaderboard ordering is not about scale.

A documented, reproducible audit of why signed Spearman is near zero on ribozymes (for example assay direction conventions or multi-mutant scoring) that changes the published ordering when corrected, with code and an honest statement of what it does and does not establish.

pitfalls: Fitting the per-assay sign or any hyperparameter on the assay's own measured values is label peeking and voids the claim, even though the leaderboard metric is signed.

Some RNAGym assays overlap sequences used to train released RNA language models; a model that memorised them is not doing zero-shot prediction, and the skeptic should check for any assay-specific fine-tuning.

The leaderboard changed metric at v0.1.1 and rescored RiNALMo and RNA-FM; quoting the older absolute-Spearman-over-all-assays numbers, or the mRNA table kept for reference, compares against a stale bar.
Picking the one category where a method happens to win and not reporting the others is cherry-picking; the criterion requires all three categories and all 31 assays.
With only 3 tRNA and 2 aptamer assays, a 0.02 macro gain can be noise; bootstrap over assays before claiming.
targets.statement: RNAGym (Rohit Arora, Murphy Angelo, Christian Choe, Courtney Shearer, Aaron Kollasch, Fiona Qu, Ruben Weitzman, Artem Gazizov, Sarah Gurev, Erik Xie, Debora Marks, Pascal Notin; bioRxiv 2025.06.16.660049) collects deep mutational scans of RNA molecules and scores zero-shot fitness predictors on them. Since leaderboard version v0.1.1 the headline metric is the signed Spearman correlation between a model's score and measured fitness, macro-averaged over three non-coding RNA categories (ribozyme 26 assays, tRNA 3, aptamer 2). In leaderboard/fitness/leaderboard_signed_3ncRNA.csv (last repository push 2026-08-14) the whole field is weak: Evo 2 (40B) leads at macro 0.2120, RNA-ERNIE 0.1937, Evo 2 (7B) 0.1904, AIDO.RNA (1.6B) 0.1824, and GenSLM is negative at -0.0338. On ribozymes, the largest category, the best value is only 0.1343 and several large models are below zero. Processed assays (73 MB), raw data, per-model predictions and alignments download over plain HTTPS from marks.hms.harvard.edu, and the aggregation script performance_fitness.py is in the repository. The open question is whether anything, including cheap non-neural baselines, does better than near-zero on ribozyme fitness.
targets.success_criterion: A score file giving one number per variant for every assay in the three ncRNA categories of RNAGym, produced by a method that never reads the assays' measured fitness values, whose macro signed Spearman over the three categories, recomputed by the skeptic with the repository's performance_fitness.py --type ncRNA, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the top macro value in leaderboard/fitness/leaderboard_signed_3ncRNA.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02 absolute, with the same method and hyperparameters applied to all 31 assays and every per-category value reported, not only the winning one.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads fitness_processed_assays.zip (73 MB) and, if needed, fitness_MSAs.zip from marks.hms.harvard.edu over plain HTTPS, checks the submitted score file covers every variant of every ncRNA assay exactly once, runs the repository's merge_scoring_files.py and performance_fitness.py --type ncRNA, and compares with the live leaderboard CSV. Minutes for scoring; the attacker pays for inference.

angles: The leaders are mixtures of finite-context models with neural mixing; the remaining redundancy is mostly long-range repeats, so add an explicit repeat-aware match model with a large hash and let the mixer arbitrate.

Cross-domain import (text compression contests): techniques from the Hutter-prize lineage, such as two-pass parameter tuning and context-mixing with SSE stages, have not been fully ported to four-symbol alphabets.

Cross-domain import (database systems): tune for the memory hierarchy, since the practical limit here is RAM and cache misses rather than model quality; a smaller model that fits in cache can afford more passes.

Exploit biology the general compressors ignore: satellite arrays and segmental duplications, newly complete in T2T, are highly structured, and a model keyed on tandem-repeat period could pay for itself.
Measure where the bits actually go per chromosome arm and attack only the worst region, rather than tuning the global average.
targets.name: T2T human genome compression: beat the best bits-per-base entry in the public human-genome compression table

partial_wins.statement: Reproduce the top JARVIS3 entry's byte count from its replication script on commodity hardware and publish the timing and memory, confirming the record is reproducible (the top row's time and memory are listed as unknown).
Beat the best entry on the companion Cassava genome table (github.com/cobilab/CassavaGenome, top entry JARVIS2 at 69,078,516 bytes / 0.7249 bits per base) under the same round-trip rule.

Beat the best general-purpose compressor entry (nncp at 1.514 bits per base) with a method that uses under 2 GB of RAM and finishes in under two hours, which would make strong DNA compression practical on a laptop.

pitfalls: Shipping a model trained on the same genome, or on a reference that contains it, and not counting that model's size, is the classic false win; the total must include everything needed to decompress.
Decompression must be exact and must be demonstrated, not asserted; a compressor that loses line breaks, case, or ambiguity codes is not comparable to the table entries.
The table's entries use a specific symbol stream (DNA symbols only, as the scripts prepare it); comparing a FASTA-file size against a symbol-stream size is apples to oranges.
Runtime matters for reproducibility but not for the ranking, so a 100x slower entry still counts; say so honestly instead of implying practicality.
The top row currently lists unknown time and memory; the claim must compare against its byte count as published, and the skeptic should note if the row changes.
targets.statement: The cobilab human-genome compression table (github.com/cobilab/HumanGenome, maintained by Diogo Pratas and colleagues) is a ranked record table for lossless reference-free compression of the T2T CHM13 v2.0 human genome: 3,117,292,120 DNA symbols, baseline 2 bits per symbol. The current top entry is JARVIS3 at 538,155,679 bytes (1.381 bits per base), followed by a reproducible JARVIS3 run at 539,129,963 bytes (1.384, 641 minutes, 13.7 GB RAM), several JARVIS2 entries near 1.395, GeCo3 near 1.425, and general-purpose compressors far behind (nncp 1.514, paq8l 1.571, zstd/lzma around 1.66). Every entry links a replication script, the sequence is a public S3 object, and the JARVIS3 paper (Maria J. P. Sousa, Armando J. Pinho, Diogo Pratas, Bioinformatics 2024) describes this as the best result to date on this benchmark. Verification is a byte count plus an exact round-trip decompression, which is as mechanical as a record check gets.
targets.success_criterion: A compressor (source code released, deterministic, no network access at run time, no reference genome or external sequence database embedded beyond what the entry declares) that losslessly compresses the chm13v2.0 DNA symbol stream, as defined by the table's own scripts, to STRICTLY FEWER bytes (direction: min) than the top entry in the table at https://github.com/cobilab/HumanGenome (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), with the decompressed output byte-identical to the input, the model size included in the reported total, and the full command line and hardware stated. A margin of at least 0.1% of the compressed size is required to exclude bookkeeping differences.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads chm13v2.0.fa.gz from the public human-pangenomics S3 bucket, prepares the symbol stream exactly as the table's scripts do, runs the claimed compressor and then its decompressor in a clean environment with no network, checks byte-identity with the original and the total output size (including any model or parameter files), and compares with the live table. Hours of compute, fully mechanical.

angles: The controls are matched on summary statistics but not on local sequence context; a model that predicts the matching variables themselves will look good and generalise badly, so build a control-matching-invariant representation on purpose and measure what is left.

Cross-domain import (information retrieval): this is a ranking problem with one positive per group of eleven, so train a listwise ranking loss within groups instead of pointwise classification, which the published logistic regressions use.

Cross-domain import (econometrics): treat fine-mapping posterior probabilities as noisy labels and fit a measurement-error model, since the positives are themselves statistical calls rather than experimentally confirmed causal variants.
Combine the released feature parquet files with simple interaction terms (conservation x predicted regulatory activity x distance) that the linear probes cannot represent, keeping everything on CPU.

Look per-trait and per-consequence subset: the repository publishes subsets such as 3_prime_UTR_variant and disease, and a method that wins on the whole set but loses on every subset is overfitting the mix.
targets.name: TraitGym complex traits: beat the best AUPRC for picking the causal regulatory variant among matched controls

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best zero-shot entry (CADD at 0.2499 as of 2026-10-15) by at least 0.02 AUPRC with a score that uses no supervised training on TraitGym labels at all.
Match or beat the best listed combination on the complex-traits set using only features that run on a laptop CPU (no Enformer or Borzoi forward passes), reusing the published feature parquet files.

A reproducible demonstration, from the public variant tables alone, that part of the remaining gap comes from control variants that are themselves plausibly causal (mismatched matching), quantified on a subset and with an honest statement of how it changes the ceiling.

pitfalls: Chromosome leakage: feature selection, hyperparameters or calibration fitted on all chromosomes and then scored by by-chromosome cross-validation inflates the result; everything must respect the chromosome split.
Reusing a model that was pretrained on the UK Biobank fine-mapping results, or on CADD scores derived from them, can smuggle the labels in; declare every external score used.
Comparing a 'matched_9' result against the 'all' (unmatched) dataset, or complex traits against Mendelian traits, compares to a different and much easier bar.
AUPRC on these group sizes is noisy; a 0.01 gain is within the published standard errors (around 0.010-0.016), hence the 0.02 margin plus bootstrap requirement.
A benchmark gain here means better prioritisation of candidate variants for follow-up, not a demonstrated causal mechanism or a clinical finding.
targets.statement: TraitGym (Gonzalo Benegas, Gokcen Eraslan, Yun S. Song; bioRxiv 2025.02.11.637758) asks a model to tell a likely causal non-coding variant from nine control variants matched on allele frequency, distance to gene and other summary statistics. The complex-traits set is built from fine-mapped UK Biobank associations across 83 traits. The main metric is AUPRC averaged over chromosomes, weighted by chromosome. In the published metric files under complex_traits_matched_9/AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average/all (75 files, read directly from the Hugging Face dataset over plain HTTPS), the best entry is the CADD+GPN-MSA+Borzoi logistic-regression combination at 0.3623 (standard error 0.0155), then CADD+Borzoi 0.3509 and GPN-MSA+Borzoi 0.3491; the best single supervised model is Enformer at 0.3033 and the best zero-shot score is CADD at 0.2499. Ten of eleven variants in each group are controls, so a perfect method would reach 1.0 and random guessing about 0.1: the field is far from solving this. All variant tables, precomputed features and per-model metric files are public; the scoring is a short Snakemake rule the skeptic can rerun.
targets.success_criterion: A score (or probability) for every variant in complex_traits_matched_9 test split, produced by a method whose feature extraction and training read no causal/control label outside the chromosomes used for training under the benchmark's own by-chromosome cross-validation, whose AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average recomputed by the skeptic with the TraitGym repository's metric rule is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best value among the published per-model CSVs in that directory and on the leaderboard space (both re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02 absolute, with a bootstrap 95% interval over chromosomes that excludes the previous best.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the dataset's test parquet and the relevant feature parquet files from the Hugging Face dataset repository over plain HTTPS (about 6.7 GB for everything, far less for one feature set), checks the submitted score file covers each variant exactly once, runs the repository's AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average computation, compares with the published per-model CSVs, and audits the code for use of labels outside the training chromosomes. Minutes.

angles: Conservation wins here, so model the thing conservation is a proxy for: predicted loss of a specific regulatory element (splice site, promoter motif, UTR structure) and combine element-type-specific scores rather than one global score.

Cross-domain import (astronomy source detection): matched controls make this a needle-in-matched-noise detection problem; borrow matched-filter thinking and build a per-trait template of what a causal variant looks like, then score by template response.
Cross-domain import (survey statistics): weight chromosomes as the metric does during model development, because a method tuned on the unweighted average optimises the wrong quantity.
Mendelian causal variants concentrate in splicing and UTRs; run a splicing-specific predictor and a UTR-structure predictor, and check whether a simple maximum of the two already beats conservation.
Compare the same score on Mendelian and complex traits: a score that wins on both is more likely to be real signal than one tuned to the rare-disease mix.
targets.name: TraitGym Mendelian traits: beat CADD zero-shot AUPRC on causal non-coding variants for rare disease

partial_wins.statement: A zero-shot score that beats phyloP-241m (0.6960 as of 2026-10-15) by at least 0.02 while using no multiple-species alignment, showing that single-sequence modelling can match conservation here.
Under the supervised (linear probing) protocol, beat CADD's 0.8747 by at least 0.02 while respecting the by-chromosome split.
A reproducible explanation, from public files only, of why adding Borzoi features to CADD lowers the Mendelian score, with a fix that recovers at least the CADD-only value.

pitfalls: CADD and several conservation scores were trained on data that overlaps the variant classes here; a new model that distils CADD is not an independent advance and must be declared.
Zero-shot means no fitting at all on TraitGym variants, including threshold or sign selection; otherwise the comparison with the zero-shot column is invalid.
The 'all' (unmatched) datasets have different class balance and much higher AUPRC values; mixing them with the matched_9 numbers is a false win.
A win on 113 Mendelian traits with per-chromosome weighting can hinge on a few chromosomes; the bootstrap requirement exists for that reason.
Better variant ranking supports, but does not constitute, a rare-disease diagnosis; every claim must say so.
targets.statement: The Mendelian half of TraitGym (Benegas, Eraslan and Song, bioRxiv 2025.02.11.637758) holds causal non-coding variants for 113 Mendelian traits, each with nine controls matched on summary statistics. In the published metric files for mendelian_traits_matched_9 (AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average, 81 files, readable over plain HTTPS), the best overall value is CADD with logistic regression at 0.8747 (standard error 0.0305), while among zero-shot scores CADD's raw score leads at 0.7122, then phyloP-241m at 0.6960 and GPN-MSA's log-likelihood ratio at 0.6945. The striking fact is that a 2014-vintage integrative score and plain conservation still beat every modern DNA language model and every functional-genomics model on this set, and that adding Borzoi to CADD lowers the score (0.7568) rather than raising it. Beating the conservation-based scores zero-shot, with a model that does not read TraitGym labels, is a clean open question that runs on a laptop from the published feature files.
targets.success_criterion: A zero-shot score for every variant in mendelian_traits_matched_9 (no training on any TraitGym label, no fitting on the benchmark's variants) whose AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average, recomputed by the skeptic with the TraitGym repository's metric rule, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best zero-shot entry among the published per-model CSVs in mendelian_traits_matched_9/AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average/all and on the leaderboard space (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02 absolute, with a bootstrap 95% interval over chromosomes excluding that previous best, and with the same score also reported on the complex-traits set.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads mendelian_traits_matched_9/test.parquet and any needed feature parquet files from Hugging Face over plain HTTPS, checks coverage of every variant, runs the official metric computation, compares with the published per-model CSVs, and greps the method's code and model card for any use of TraitGym labels or of the Mendelian variant list. Minutes.

angles: Rule learning over k-mers done better: Kover's set-covering machine is strong because resistance is sparse and rule-like. Push it with richer unitig features (compacted de Bruijn graph unitigs instead of fixed-k k-mers), explicit gene-presence features from a resistance-gene database, and rule complexity chosen by nested cross-validation inside the training folds only.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / sparse recovery): formulate presence/absence of thousands of unitigs as a sparse linear code and recover the causal support with group-LASSO or orthogonal matching pursuit, with gene-level groups; this directly targets the rare-allele regime where k-mer ML fails.

CROSS-DOMAIN (cryptanalysis-style exhaustive search): enumerate short boolean formulas (depth-2 DNF over <= 4 literals) over a reduced feature set by branch-and-bound/ILP for a globally optimal rule under the training folds, rather than greedy heuristics - small-formula exhaustive search is exactly a laptop-agents strength and gives auditable rules.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / community genomics): model the accessory genome as a species-abundance/occupancy problem and use ordination (NMDS, UMAP on Jaccard of gene content) to build phylogeny-aware covariates, then de-confound with a kinship/relatedness random effect (linear mixed model, as in bacterial GWAS) to stop the model learning clade membership instead of resistance.

CROSS-DOMAIN (information theory): rank candidate features by conditional mutual information given clade label rather than by raw association, to isolate signals that survive population-structure conditioning; complement with homoplasy counts on the core-genome tree (convergent emergence as evidence of causality).

Transfer across datasets: pool species-antibiotic datasets of the same drug class with hierarchical/multitask models so the rare-resistance datasets borrow strength, which is what the paper suggests is missing when beta-lactam performance swings wildly across species.
targets.name: AMR genotype-to-phenotype: beat the published benchmark F1 on the frozen PATRIC species-antibiotic folds

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best published ML method (excluding ResFinder) on one species-antibiotic dataset by >= 0.03 F1 on the published folds, while also reporting ResFinder's published value for context.

Beat the best published value on >= 3 datasets of the same antibiotic class (e.g. beta-lactams, where the paper reports high cross-species variance) with a single uniform model and no per-dataset tuning, with per-fold numbers.

A phylogeny-stratified re-analysis: using the published folds, quantify how each method's and the new model's F1 depends on the train-test phylogenetic distance of each genome (reproducing the paper's divergence finding), and exhibit a model that closes >= 30% of the gap between ML and ResFinder on the most divergent decile of test genomes.

pitfalls: Fold tampering: the entire value of this target is the published folds. Rebuilding folds, dropping genomes that fail download, or re-balancing classes invalidates the comparison; the skeptic must hash the fold files and compare genome-ID sets exactly.

Population-structure leakage inside folds: even with the published 'loose' folds, nested model selection done on all folds at once leaks. Hyperparameters must be chosen inside each training fold, and the code must show it.

Metric definition drift: F1 for which class, macro or micro, averaged over folds or computed on pooled predictions - these differ by several points. The paper's definition must be reproduced exactly, and the comparator is the best published method for that dataset, not the paper's average across datasets.

Dataset cherry-picking: with 78 datasets, trying all of them and reporting the one that beat its published number is multiple testing. Either pre-register the dataset or report all attempted datasets and apply a correction.

Phenotype metadata drift: PATRIC/BV-BRC phenotype records have been revised and PATRIC itself moved to BV-BRC; only the committed phenotype files in the repository may be used, never today's database values.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov now serves a reCAPTCHA page to plain requests; read the article through Europe PMC (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11070729/fullTextXML) instead of https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11070729/.

The BV-BRC genome FTP (ftp.bvbrc.org/genomes/) did not respond on 2026-10-15; fetch assemblies through NCBI/ENA accessions via the repository's PATRIC-to-NCBI mapping and log the accessions, so the genome set can be re-fetched by a stranger.
targets.statement: The HZI AMR benchmarking study (Hu et al., Briefings in Bioinformatics 2024, PMC11070729) compared Kover, PhenotypeSeeker, Seq2Geno2Pheno, Aytan-Aktug, an ML baseline and rule-based ResFinder across 78 species-antibiotic datasets built from PATRIC. Crucially, the repository github.com/hzi-bifo/AMR_benchmarking (last commit 2024-11-29) publishes the exact genome lists, phenotype metadata and EVALUATION FOLDS (data/PATRIC/cv_folds/loose) plus the PATRIC-to-NCBI accession mapping, so anyone can reproduce the identical cross-validation partitions without rerunning the (cluster-scale) baseline pipelines. The paper's headline findings - ML methods degrade on phylogenetically divergent strains, ResFinder wins there, Kover is usually the best ML method, beta-lactam predictions are erratic across species - define a clear per-dataset frontier. The paper prioritises F1-macro (and, for the clinical view, F1 and precision on the susceptible class); the per-dataset numbers live in its supplementary spreadsheets, not the article body. Beating a published F1 on a fixed fold set with only variant/k-mer features from public assemblies is laptop work for the smaller species-antibiotic combinations.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for at least one species-antibiotic dataset of the benchmark, a released model evaluated on the EXACT published folds (the committed fold files of the single_S_A_folds family, https://github.com/hzi-bifo/AMR_benchmarking/tree/main/data/PATRIC/cv_folds/loose/single_S_A_folds/<species>/<antibiotic>, verified by sha256 and by genome-ID set comparison), trained only on each fold's training genomes (public assemblies fetched by the repo's own retrieval script) and the published phenotype metadata, whose cross-validated F1-macro (the paper's primary metric; a claim on the clinically oriented susceptible-class F1 or precision must say so and compare against that same published column) computed with the same definition and averaging as the paper is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published value for that dataset across ALL benchmarked methods including ResFinder, read live immediately before claiming from the per-dataset supplementary tables (supplementary_table_s2..s10_bbae206.xlsx, served by https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11070729/supplementaryFiles; the article body itself carries only summary tables), by at least 0.03 absolute AND outside a 95% bootstrap interval over folds. The result must be reported per dataset, with per-fold values, confusion matrices and the fold-file hashes; averaging over a self-chosen subset of the 78 datasets does not count.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones hzi-bifo/AMR_benchmarking at a pinned commit, hashes the fold and phenotype files, downloads the assemblies for one dataset through NCBI/ENA accessions using the repository's PATRIC-to-NCBI mapping (hundreds to a few thousand genomes, a few GB; the BV-BRC FTP timed out on 2026-10-15 and is not a reliable route), reruns the attacker's released training/prediction code fold by fold on the skeptic's machine, recomputes F1 with the paper's definition (and recomputes ResFinder's calls with the public ResFinder database as a sanity check), bootstraps over folds, and re-reads the published per-dataset values from the supplementary spreadsheets. No GPU and no 370 GB baseline reproduction is needed because the folds and the published numbers are the comparator.

angles: Ensemble the existing public predictors properly: CAID3's own analysis shows method rankings vary by category and by negative-set definition, so a calibrated stacking (per-residue logistic/isotonic fusion fitted on CAID1/CAID2 references only, never CAID3) of freely available CPU predictors (IUPred, MobiDB-lite, flDPnn-class, AlphaFold-disorder pLDDT/RSA) is a cheap shot at the frontier.

AlphaFold-derived features at scale: BioComputingUP's own AlphaFold-disorder work shows pLDDT plus predicted relative solvent accessibility is a strong disorder signal; AlphaFold DB models for all reference targets are free to download, so a feature-engineering sweep over smoothing windows and per-residue contact-density is laptop work.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing): treat per-residue property tracks (charge, hydropathy, complexity) as a 1-D signal and apply matched filters / wavelet multiresolution analysis to detect disorder boundaries; CAID scores boundaries implicitly through average precision, so edge-accurate segmentation (change-point detection, e.g. PELT or Bayesian online change-point) should pay off more than per-residue classification.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / linguistics): low-complexity and compositional bias are hallmarks of disorder; use universal-compressor code length per window (CTW/PPM), entropy-rate estimates, and Zipf/Heaps statistics of k-mer usage as features, plus 'linguistic' detection of repeat grammars (tandem repeats, SLiM-like motifs) for the binding sub-challenge.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics): score disorder from a coarse-grained polymer/Flory-type model, predicting per-residue order parameters from sequence charge decoration (kappa, sequence charge decoration SCD) and temperature-like effective solvent terms, which is analytic and instant on CPU.

Binding sub-challenge specifics: mine public motif resources (ELM classes) and conditional folding signals (AlphaFold models of disordered regions in complex contexts) to score binding propensity within annotated disordered boundaries, the category the assessment calls still weak.
targets.name: CAID3 (Critical Assessment of Intrinsic Disorder): beat the published best average precision on the frozen CAID3 reference

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best published CAID3 average precision in a binding sub-challenge (the weakest categories, explicitly flagged as unsolved) by >= 0.02 with the official scorer on the rebuilt reference: Binding-IDR (best 0.514, the less imbalanced binding bar) or Binding (best 0.249), even if the disorder categories are not improved.

Match the top-5 published CAID3 disorder average precision to within 0.01 with a predictor that uses NO protein language model and no GPU-trained network (e.g. physicochemical + alignment statistics only), running the full reference in under 30 minutes on a laptop, with timings.

A reproducible negative-control audit: show that the published ranking order of at least 3 CAID3 methods flips when the reference is rebuilt with a documented, defensible choice of negative-set definition (NOX vs PDB-derived negatives), quantified with the official scorer and bootstrap intervals; a methodology finding, reported as such, not a record.

pitfalls: Reference mismatch: CAID3's official reference is a specific DisProt snapshot with a specific negative-set choice; rebuilding it from today's DisProt silently changes the labels (DisProt grows monthly) and can inflate or deflate APS. The skeptic must rebuild from the frozen release used by CAID3 and hash the files, or the comparison is void.

Hidden training on the test labels: nearly all modern disorder predictors are trained on DisProt/PDB-missing-residue data; if the attacker's model (or any ensemble component, including a downloaded web-server predictor) was trained after the CAID3 freeze, the CAID3 targets are in its training set and the whole result is leakage.

Metric substitution: CAID ranks by average precision on a specific target set and aggregation; reporting AUC-ROC, balanced accuracy, or a per-residue micro-average over pooled residues will look better and means nothing. Also disorder is heavily imbalanced, so ROC numbers are deceptively high.
Dropping hard targets or short proteins, or predicting only within regions where another predictor is confident, changes the denominator; every target in the category must be scored.
Treating the CAID3 paper's headline improvement percentages as the bar instead of the per-category best APS value in the ranking table; the record must reference the live table and a direction (max).

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov now serves a reCAPTCHA page to plain requests; read the article through Europe PMC (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12750029/fullTextXML) instead of https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12750029/.
targets.statement: CAID is the community blind assessment of intrinsic-disorder and disorder-binding predictors run by the BioComputingUP group; round 3 (CAID3, assessed with CASP16, results published 2025) assessed 68 methods on a reference built from DisProt annotations that were not public when predictions were submitted, in categories Disorder-NOX, Disorder-PDB, Binding, Linker and the new Binding-IDR sub-challenge (same proteins and positives as Binding, negatives restricted to disordered non-binding residues, 72.6% of residues excluded), which is the honest, less imbalanced binding bar. Best published average precision (APS) per category, parsed from the Europe PMC full text on 2026-10-15: Disorder-NOX 0.754 (ESMDisPred-2PDB, AUC 0.885); Disorder-PDB 0.928 (PUNCH2, AUC 0.955); Binding 0.249 (IPA-AF2-Protein-bind, AUC 0.775); Binding-IDR 0.514 (bindEmbed21IDR-rawGeneral, AUC 0.641); Linker 0.474 (IPA-AF2-Linker, AUC 0.897). Protein misfolding/aggregation and disorder are directly implicated in neurodegenerative disease, and the CAID3 report itself states that binding-region prediction within known disordered boundaries 'remains challenging', i.e. the metric is far from saturated. The assessment code (BioComputingUP/CAID, caid.py plus vectorized_metrics) and the reference-construction code (BioComputingUP/caid-reference, last pushed 2026-08-13; also caid2-reference) are public on GitHub, so the whole evaluation can be reproduced on a laptop from DisProt plus SIFTS. No CAID4 round was found to be open as of 2026-10-13, which makes this a frozen, fully public held-out benchmark rather than a live submission system.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released predictor (code + weights + fixed inference command) whose per-residue scores for the entire CAID3 reference set, scored by the official assessment code (github.com/BioComputingUP/CAID, pinned commit, the same metric implementation and the same reference files the paper used, rebuilt with github.com/BioComputingUP/caid-reference from the DisProt release CAID3 froze), give an average precision STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published CAID3 value for that same category and reference subset, read live from the CAID3 assessment paper's ranking table at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12750029/fullTextXML immediately before claiming (as of 2026-10-15: Disorder-NOX 0.754, Disorder-PDB 0.928, Binding 0.249, Binding-IDR 0.514, Linker 0.474), by at least 0.02 absolute AND by more than the bootstrap standard error the skeptic computes by resampling targets (1,000 resamples). The predictor must use no DisProt annotation newer than the CAID3 freeze, must not query any web server whose training data is unknown, and must be run on all targets of the category with no target dropped and no per-target tuning. Reporting a different metric (AUC instead of APS, or per-residue instead of the official aggregation) does not count.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones BioComputingUP/CAID and BioComputingUP/caid-reference at pinned commits, rebuilds the CAID3 reference from the frozen DisProt release plus SIFTS (both public), hashes the reference files, runs caid.py's vectorized metrics on the attacker's prediction files (CAID submission format, one score per residue for every target), bootstraps over targets for an error bar, and re-reads the published CAID3 ranking table. Reproducibility check: rerun the attacker's released inference on 50 random targets and compare scores bit-for-bit (or within documented tolerance). All steps are CPU-only and under an hour.

angles: Label-efficiency over architecture: with a few dozen positives per rare class, class-balanced losses, focal loss and threshold selection on a held-out slice of the TRAINING data (never CODE-test) usually buy more F1 than a bigger network.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing): classical ECG engineering - baseline wander removal, QRS detection, beat alignment and template subtraction, RR-interval irregularity statistics - still beats raw deep learning for atrial fibrillation and bradycardia, and runs instantly on CPU.

CROSS-DOMAIN (time-series / point processes): model the RR-interval sequence as a point process and test for the loss of regularity (sample entropy, Poincare dispersion, Markov-order tests) - atrial fibrillation is a rhythm problem, not a morphology problem.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression): normalised compression distance between a beat template and class-specific dictionaries gives a near-parameter-free classifier that is robust to amplitude scaling across recording devices.

Calibration and decision policy: F1 depends on the operating point, so per-class threshold optimisation on training data, conformal prediction and reporting the full precision-recall curve is where honest gains live.
Transfer from the public CODE-15% release (Zenodo 4916206) with careful de-duplication against the test exams, which is the only large public source of the same acquisition pipeline.
targets.name: CODE-test 12-lead ECG: beat the published per-abnormality F1 on the 827-exam annotated test set

partial_wins.statement: Beat the reference network's published F1 on one of the rare classes (1st-degree AV block or atrial fibrillation) with the bootstrap interval excluding zero and no degradation elsewhere.

Match the reference network's published F1 on all six classes to within 0.01 using a model with under 100k parameters that trains in under 2 hours on a CPU, with code and timings - an efficiency result for low-resource settings.

A reproduction and uncertainty audit: recompute the published per-class metrics for the released reference weights on CODE-test, publish the bootstrap intervals the original report does not give, and document which published differences between the model and the human annotators are inside noise.

pitfalls: Test-set reuse: the 827 exams are tiny and heavily reused in the literature; tuning thresholds, early stopping or model selection on CODE-test is the standard false positive here and must be shown absent in code.
Patient overlap with CODE-15%: the same patients can appear in the public training release; exam and patient identifiers must be checked disjoint, or the result is memorisation.
Multiplicity: six classes times many architectures means some class will look better by chance; the margin must survive a bootstrap over exams and the no-degradation rule for the other five classes.

Metric mismatch: the published numbers use a specific threshold and averaging; comparing a tuned-threshold F1 to a default-threshold published F1, or a macro-average to a per-class value, is not a win.
This is an annotated-benchmark gain, not evidence of clinical safety: the labels are consensus annotations on 10-second tracings from one country's screening programme.
targets.statement: Antonio H. Ribeiro and colleagues released CODE-test (Zenodo record 3765780, data.zip 218 MB, CC-licensed, no registration): 827 twelve-lead ECG tracings from the Brazilian CODE study, each annotated by consensus of cardiologists for six abnormalities (1st-degree AV block, right and left bundle branch block, sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation). The companion paper (Nat Commun 11:1760, 2020) and the code at github.com/antonior92/automatic-ecg-diagnosis publish per-abnormality precision, recall, specificity and F1 for a residual network and for cardiology residents, medical students and emergency physicians on exactly this test set, with model weights public on Zenodo. Because the test labels, the tracings and the reference model are all public and the set is tiny, a stranger's laptop can rescore any new model in minutes - and the rare classes (AV block, atrial fibrillation; a few dozen positives each) are where the published F1 is weakest and where the honest uncertainty is largest.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released model plus a saved per-exam, per-class score file for all 827 CODE-test exams (no exam dropped; sha256 of the score file published), trained only on data that excludes CODE-test (the public CODE-15% release or other public ECG corpora; the training exam identifiers must be released and checked disjoint from CODE-test), such that for at least one of the six abnormalities the F1 computed with the repository's own evaluation code is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the published value for the reference neural network on that abnormality, re-read live from the paper and from https://github.com/antonior92/automatic-ecg-diagnosis immediately before claiming, by a margin whose 95% bootstrap interval over exams excludes zero, while NO other abnormality's F1 falls by more than 0.01. Precision, recall, specificity and the confusion matrix must be reported per class; with only 827 exams, a claim without the interval over exams is not a result.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads CODE-test from Zenodo (one 218 MB zip, plain HTTPS), hashes it, runs the attacker's released model to regenerate the score file (bit-for-bit or within a documented tolerance), recomputes per-class precision/recall/F1 with the repository's evaluation script, bootstraps over exams, re-runs the published reference weights as a control to confirm the published numbers reproduce on the skeptic's machine, and checks the released training-identifier list is disjoint from CODE-test. Minutes on CPU.

angles: Backfill modelling: the first-reported value for the last week is revised upward systematically; learn the revision distribution from the vintages and nowcast it, which is where much of the ensemble's horizon -1/0 error comes from.
Performance-weighted ensembling of the other submitted models using only past scores at each date (trailing-window relative WIS), with shrinkage toward equal weights.

Cross-domain import (electricity load forecasting): quantile regression averaging (QRA) and conformal recalibration of quantiles on a rolling window, standard tools in energy forecasting competitions.

Cross-domain import (hydrology): treat hospital admissions as a routed flow with lagged upstream signals; use NSSP emergency-department visit percentages (also in the hub, with vintages) as a leading indicator.
Hierarchical reconciliation: forecast states and the nation jointly and reconcile (MinT) so that state quantiles and the national forecast are coherent.
targets.name: US COVID-19 Forecast Hub: beat the hub ensemble's season-average WIS for hospital admissions in a vintage-honest retrospective

partial_wins.statement: Beat the ensemble's mean WIS by >= 3% at horizons 0-1 (nowcast and one week ahead) over a full season under the vintage rule.
Beat the ensemble at the national level only (location US) over a full season, horizons 0-3.
A re-weighted ensemble of the hub's own submissions (weights fitted only on past weeks at each date) that beats the equal-weight CovidHub-ensemble.

pitfalls: Using final (oracle) data as inputs for past dates is the classic retrospective leak; only as_of-filtered vintages count, and the skeptic must log file access.
Comparing on a different task set (dropping hard locations or weeks) flatters any model; the comparison must be on exactly the rows the ensemble forecast.
WIS conventions (which quantiles, scaling, log transform) change rankings; use the hubverse implementation and state the variant.
A single good season can be luck; the paired bootstrap over reference dates is required.
This is a forecasting-method benchmark, not public-health guidance.
targets.statement: The CDC-run COVID-19 Forecast Hub (github.com/CDCgov/covid19-forecast-hub, pushed 2026-10-13) collects weekly quantile forecasts of laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 hospital admissions (NHSN) for the US, 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico, horizons -1 to 3 weeks, from tens of models, with the CovidHub-ensemble from 2024-11-23 onward and a CovidHub-baseline. Because all submitted forecasts, the oracle (final) truth and a time-series of data VINTAGES (target-data/time-series.parquet, with as_of dates) are public, one can build a forecaster that, at each past reference date, sees only the data available then, and compare its weighted interval score (WIS) to the ensemble's. The ensemble is notoriously hard to beat; the question is whether a principled method beats it over a full season.
targets.success_criterion: For one complete season (2024-25 from 2024-11-23, or 2025-26), quantile forecasts in hub format for every (reference_date, location, horizon 0-3) for which CovidHub-ensemble submitted, generated by a frozen pipeline that at each reference date uses only data with as_of <= that date's Wednesday deadline (from target-data/time-series.parquet), whose mean WIS against target-data/oracle-output.parquet (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than CovidHub-ensemble's mean WIS on exactly the same task set by at least 3% relative, with a paired bootstrap over reference dates excluding zero. Other teams' forecasts may be used only if their file dates are on or before the reference date.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the hub (or reads it via the public S3 mirror with --no-sign-request), re-runs the attacker's pipeline in a loop over reference dates with a data loader that filters time-series.parquet by as_of, checks no file dated after each reference date is touched (file-access log), scores both models with the hubverse WIS implementation on the identical task set, and bootstraps. Laptop-hours.

angles: Use the score decomposition as a map: scores.csv separates sharpness from under- and overprediction per model and country, so the attacker can see exactly where the ensemble pays - usually overprediction after peaks - and design for that.

CROSS-DOMAIN (renewal theory / statistical physics): a renewal-process model with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck reproduction number propagates uncertainty analytically and avoids the overconfident curve fits that WIS punishes.
CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing): complex demodulation or a Kalman filter on log-incidence estimates phase and amplitude separately, and epidemic turning points are phase problems.

CROSS-DOMAIN (econometrics): forecast combination with time-varying weights estimated by exponentially weighted performance (the standard model-averaging literature) applied only to past scores at each date, with shrinkage to equal weights.

CROSS-DOMAIN (MDL / prequential model selection): choose among candidate forecast families online by predictive code length rather than hindsight fit - the discipline that keeps retrospective wins honest.
Hierarchical pooling across countries and waves, which is where small-country WIS is won; the ensemble averages models, not information.
targets.name: European COVID-19 Forecast Hub archive: beat EuroCOVIDhub-ensemble's WIS on the hub's own published scores

partial_wins.statement: Strictly lower mean WIS than EuroCOVIDhub-baseline AND than the median submitted model over the declared period and target, under the as-of discipline, with the bootstrap interval excluding zero.
Beat the ensemble on the subset of smaller countries (bottom half by mean reported count), where ensembles are typically weakest, across all forecast dates of the declared period.

An independent scoring reproduction: recompute the published per-model WIS decomposition in scores.csv from data-processed and the truth data, documenting every model whose recomputed value differs by more than 1% and why.

pitfalls: Final-data leakage: training or fitting on the revised series while calling the exercise retrospective is the classic false positive; only dated snapshots may be read and the audit must show it.

Hindsight tuning: selecting the model family, window or spread multiplier after seeing the period's scores is overfitting dressed as forecasting; parameters must be frozen on an earlier period with commit evidence.
Row mismatch: the ensemble did not submit every week for every country; the comparison must be on exactly its rows, with the hub's exclusion rules.
Scoring conventions: WIS depends on the quantile set, counts versus rates and the averaging order; reproducing the published ensemble values first is the only way to know the scorer matches.
Ensemble contamination: consuming other teams' submissions for the same period turns the result into a post-hoc combination, not a forecaster.
A retrospective WIS gain on a closed hub is a methods result; it is not evidence about any future epidemic.
targets.statement: The European COVID-19 Forecast Hub ran from 2021 to autumn 2024 and is now archived at github.com/european-modelling-hubs/covid19-forecast-hub-europe_archive, with every submitted forecast in data-processed, the truth data, and - crucially - its own evaluation/scores.csv, a 2.8 MB file holding WIS, its sharpness/under- and overprediction decomposition, absolute error, bias and interval coverage for every model, forecast date, horizon and country (31,256 rows covering 2023-10-30 to 2024-09-16 as fetched 2026-10-15), including EuroCOVIDhub-ensemble and EuroCOVIDhub-baseline. Nikos Bosse, Katharine Sherratt and colleagues' evaluation of this hub (PMC10238088, 2023) found the ensemble hard to beat, which is exactly the standing question. Everything needed for a frozen, vintage-honest retrospective is public and small, and because the hub is closed the comparison can never drift under the claimant's feet.
targets.success_criterion: Success means saved quantile forecasts, in the hub's submission format, covering every (model-free) forecast_date, location, target_variable and horizon for which EuroCOVIDhub-ensemble has a row in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/european-modelling-hubs/covid19-forecast-hub-europe_archive/main/evaluation/scores.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) for one declared target_variable and one declared continuous period of at least six months, produced by a deterministic pipeline that at each forecast date uses only data available then (the hub's dated truth snapshots; no final revised series, no other team's submissions, no parameter tuned on later weeks), whose mean WIS, recomputed by the skeptic with the public scoringutils/hubverse implementation on the identical rows, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the ensemble's by at least 3% relative, with a stationary bootstrap over forecast dates at 90% excluding zero. The scorer must first reproduce the ensemble's published WIS from the raw forecasts and truth to within 1%.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the archive at a pinned commit, validates the attacker's forecast files against the hub format, recomputes WIS for the attacker, the ensemble and the baseline with public scoring code (first reproducing published values as a scorer check), bootstraps over forecast dates, and audits for look-ahead by rerunning the attacker's pipeline against truncated truth snapshots and by grepping the code for reads of future weeks, of scores.csv or of data-processed. The repository is a few hundred megabytes; the check is CPU-minutes.

angles: Catalogue-plus-residual modelling: start from the WHO catalogue as a feature (not a competitor), then learn a sparse residual model over remaining variants in the candidate gene set; most of the achievable gain is in isolates the catalogue calls susceptible by absence of evidence.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / group testing): resistance is caused by rare variants in a known gene set, which is a sparse-recovery problem. Use compressed-sensing / LASSO-type sparse recovery with group structure by gene and codon, and design the feature matrix like a pooling design so that rare alleles with few carriers are still identifiable.

CROSS-DOMAIN (cryptanalysis / combinatorial search): treat resistance rules as a small boolean formula over variant indicators and search the rule space directly (set-cover, SAT/ILP, or Kover-style rule learning) to get human-readable DNF rules; this is exactly the kind of exhaustive small-formula search laptop agents does well, and the rules are auditable.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / epistasis): fit a Potts/Ising model over co-occurring variants within and across genes to capture compensatory mutations (e.g. rpoA/rpoC with rpoB), modelling resistance as a threshold phenomenon in an interaction network rather than an additive sum.

CROSS-DOMAIN (phylogenetics as confound control): use the isolate phylogeny from the joint-genotyped VCFs both to build honest cluster-aware splits and as a covariate (homoplasy counting: variants that arise independently many times on the tree are mechanistically resistance-associated, a convergence signal that beats raw association).

MIC regression rather than binary classification: the compendium ships MICs, so model the full dose-response ladder (ordinal regression across dilutions) and derive binary calls at the published ECOFF; ordinal information sharply increases effective sample size for the rare-resistance drugs.
targets.name: Tuberculosis drug resistance from genotype: beat the WHO catalogue head-to-head on the public CRyPTIC compendium

partial_wins.statement: For one of the newer/second-line drugs where the catalogue is weakest (BDQ, DLM, CFZ, LZD or ETH), a held-out cluster-aware split result with sensitivity at least 10 points above the WHO catalogue at equal-or-better specificity, with bootstrap intervals and full confusion matrices.

A reproducible leakage demonstration: show that a random (non-cluster-aware) split inflates held-out performance for the same model and drug by a quantified margin versus the cluster-aware split, with the split files and code released - the standard trap in this dataset, reported as a methodology result.

A ranked list of >= 10 candidate resistance-associated variants (gene, position, allele) that are absent from the stated WHO catalogue version but reach a pre-registered association threshold on the TRAINING split only and then replicate on the untouched held-out split, with effect sizes, counts and a multiple-testing correction.

pitfalls: Population-structure leakage: M. tuberculosis is clonal, so random train/test splits put near-identical isolates on both sides and inflate performance enormously. Only lineage/cluster-aware splits count, and the skeptic must recompute the clusters.

Phenotype noise and quality flags: binary calls derive from MICs near the ECOFF with LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH quality; choosing the quality filter after seeing results, or filtering the attacker's test set differently from the catalogue's, manufactures gains. Filters must be pre-registered and identical for both predictors.

Class imbalance theatre: for BDQ, DLM, LZD and CFZ resistance prevalence is a fraction of a percent, so AUROC and accuracy look superb for a trivial model. Report sensitivity at matched specificity with confusion matrices and bootstrap intervals, never accuracy or AUROC alone.

Catalogue version drift and circularity: the WHO catalogue was derived partly from CRyPTIC data, so isolates used in its derivation are not neutral ground; the comparison must name the catalogue version and acknowledge that the catalogue is itself partially fitted to this cohort (which, if anything, biases against the attacker, but it must be stated).

Scope creep into clinical claims: any statement about what a clinician should do, or any per-patient interpretation, is out of bounds for this lane; the deliverable is a prediction table and metrics on public isolates.
targets.statement: The CRyPTIC compendium (EBI FTP, release June 2022) gives Mycobacterium tuberculosis clinical isolates (one per row of the pinned reuse table CRyPTIC_reuse_table_20240917.csv; the claim must state the row count of that file) with per-drug binary resistance phenotypes and MICs for 13 drugs (AMI, BDQ, CFZ, DLM, EMB, ETH, INH, KAN, LEV, LZD, MXF, RIF, RFB), phenotype quality flags, ENA accessions and paths to per-sample VCFs and joint-genotyped VCFs. The clinically deployed comparator is the WHO mutation catalogue, a fixed, public look-up table whose sensitivity is poor for the newer and second-line drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid, clofazimine, linezolid, pyrazinamide, ethionamide). Genotype-to-phenotype prediction for exactly those drugs is a live open problem, the inputs are variant calls (not reads), so the data is gigabytes rather than terabytes, and a head-to-head on identical held-out isolates is mechanically checkable. This is drug-resistance epidemiology, not treatment advice: the output is a prediction table, never a recommendation for any patient.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for at least one drug, a released model plus a saved per-isolate prediction file on a held-out test split of the CRyPTIC reuse table (split defined BEFORE training by a published rule that is lineage/phylogeny-aware - isolates grouped by genomic cluster so no cluster spans train and test - and fixed by a committed split file with sha256), using only the public VCFs/variant calls and the pinned reuse table CRyPTIC_reuse_table_20240917.csv (sha256 logged; the reuse/ directory holds five dated tables with real content changes between them, and DLM_PHENOTYPE_QUALITY exists only from the 20231208 table onward), such that on that held-out split the model's sensitivity is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the WHO catalogue's sensitivity computed on the SAME isolates and the same phenotype column, at specificity no lower than the WHO catalogue's on those isolates, with both differences outside a 95% bootstrap interval over isolates (and over clusters). Phenotype quality filtering must follow the compendium's documented rule, be stated in advance and applied identically to both predictors. The claim must be stated per drug, must report the exact catalogue version and the ECOFF used, and must present the full confusion matrices. No clinical or treatment interpretation may be attached; MIC/phenotype prediction only.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the pinned CRyPTIC_reuse_table_20240917.csv from the EBI FTP (plain HTTPS, 5.1 MB) and checks its sha256, then the per-sample VCFs for the test-split isolates (paths in the table are relative to reuse/ and point into ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/cryptic/release_june2022/reproducibility/, where the multi-gigabyte part of the download lives), verifies the committed split file's sha256 and that it is cluster-aware (recompute clusters from the joint-genotyped VCFs by SNP distance and check no cluster spans train/test), runs the attacker's released model on the test VCFs to regenerate predictions (bit-for-bit or within documented tolerance), implements the WHO catalogue look-up independently on the same VCFs, and computes both confusion matrices, sensitivity/specificity and bootstrap intervals over isolates and clusters. CPU-only, well under an hour once the VCFs are local.
