angles: Treat the three targets as one joint distribution: simulate full season trajectories and derive peak height, peak week and season total from the same posterior, instead of fitting three separate predictors - coherence alone improves log scores.

CROSS-DOMAIN (hydrology): seasonal streamflow forecasting faces the identical problem (predict a peak and its timing from a partially observed season) and its ensemble-streamflow-prediction trick - splice the observed season onto all historical remainders, then weight the analogues - is a strong, nearly parameter-free baseline.

CROSS-DOMAIN (climate science): dengue transmission tracks temperature, rainfall and ENSO indices with lags; the challenge ships the environmental series, and lagged-covariate selection with proper out-of-sample discipline is underused.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / renewal processes): serotype-structured susceptibility makes successive seasons dependent; a renewal model with a susceptible-depletion state captures the alternation that pure time-series models miss.

CROSS-DOMAIN (information theory): the score is a log score, so the task is density estimation, not point prediction - mixture densities, tail inflation and explicit mass on 'no epidemic' outcomes are where the score is won.
Borrow across the two cities: San Juan has a much longer record than Iquitos, so hierarchical pooling of seasonal shape parameters regularises the short series.
targets.name: Dengue Forecasting Project (San Juan and Iquitos): beat the published forecast skill on the frozen 2015 challenge targets

partial_wins.statement: Beat the published historical-average baseline on all three targets for BOTH cities under the challenge's data rule, with bootstrap intervals - something several original submissions did not achieve.
Beat the best published score for peak week (the timing target, where the published skill is lowest) in one city, with the full predictive distributions released.

A reproduction result: recompute the published per-team scores from the challenge's archived forecasts and the public truth series with a released scorer, documenting any discrepancy and its cause (score truncation rule, binning, missing weeks).

pitfalls: Hindsight data: the whole series is public today, so it is trivially easy to fit on the future of the season being forecast; only the challenge's as-of rule counts, with a file-access audit.
Score definition: the challenge's logarithmic score uses specific bins and a truncation floor for zero-probability outcomes; changing the binning or the floor can swamp any real gain.
Target cherry-picking: six city/target combinations invite selective reporting; all must be reported, and the baseline comparison must accompany every claim.
Tiny samples: a handful of seasons means season-level luck dominates, so intervals over forecast weeks and, ideally, a leave-one-season-out replication are required before any claim.
Old data: these are 1990s-2010s series from two cities; a skill gain is a methods result about this benchmark and carries no implication for current dengue control anywhere.
targets.statement: Dengue is the neglected-tropical-disease side of epidemic forecasting and has almost none of the infrastructure that influenza enjoys. The 2015 U.S. interagency Dengue Forecasting Project, analysed by Michael Johansson and colleagues in PNAS (open access, Europe PMC PMC6883829, 2019), remains the cleanest fully public benchmark: weekly case series, environmental and population data for San Juan (Puerto Rico) and Iquitos (Peru) are in github.com/cdcepi/dengue-forecasting-project-2015, the three targets (peak incidence, peak week, season total) and the probabilistic scoring rule (logarithmic score) are fixed and published, and the paper reports the skill achieved by every participating team and by a simple historical-average baseline, with the finding that many models failed to beat that baseline for several targets. Everything is kilobytes of CSV; the open question is whether modern methods beat the published skill under the challenge's own rules.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released, deterministic pipeline plus saved probabilistic forecasts in the challenge's own format for ALL seasons, both cities and all three targets of the challenge, produced under the challenge's data rule - at each forecast week only data available then (the challenge's delivery schedule and the dated case series) and no data from the forecast season's future - whose mean logarithmic score, computed with the challenge's scoring definition by a scorer the skeptic reruns, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max, scores are log probabilities) than the best published mean score for that city and target, re-read live from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC6883829/fullTextXML immediately before claiming, by a margin whose 95% bootstrap interval over forecast weeks excludes zero, AND strictly greater than the published historical-average baseline on the same rows. Results must be reported for all six city/target combinations; reporting only the combination that improved is not a result.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones cdcepi/dengue-forecasting-project-2015, hashes the case and covariate series, reruns the attacker's pipeline week by week against a data loader truncated at each delivery date (file-access log checked), recomputes logarithmic scores with the challenge definition including its binning and truncation rules, bootstraps over forecast weeks, and re-reads the published skill table through Europe PMC. Kilobytes of data, minutes of CPU.

angles: Conventional: calibration-free targets. Train on within-study ranks or on per-drug standardised responses so the model never has to transfer an absolute lnIC50 scale, then map back with only training-study statistics; most of the cross-study MSE is scale and concentration-range mismatch.
Conventional: robust feature spaces - pathway-level or rank-transformed expression features that are invariant to platform differences between CCLE-derived and Sanger-derived omics.

Cross-domain import (signal processing / channel equalisation): treat the external screen as the same signal passed through a different measurement channel and fit a blind equaliser (quantile-matching / histogram equalisation estimated from UNLABELLED external features only) to the prediction distribution; blind, label-free equalisation is legitimate transductive calibration and is exactly the tool for a scale-mismatch channel.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics of generalisation / domain-shift geometry): measure the covariate shift between studies with a spectral distance between omics covariance matrices, then reweight training samples by an importance ratio estimated in the leading eigen-directions (kernel mean matching); this is the principled version of 'train on the cell lines that look like the target screen'.

Cross-domain import (ecology / rank-abundance statistics): compare per-drug response distributions across screens as rank-abundance curves and transfer only the ordinal structure, scoring with Spearman-oriented losses; ecology has well-developed tools for comparing community compositions measured with different effort.

Ensembles across model families with disagreement-based abstention, measuring whether the best achievable cross-study metric comes from a single family or from averaging; cheap and directly testable with saved predictions.
targets.name: DrEval cross-study generalisation: beat the public best CTRPv2-to-GDSC2 (and CCLE/GDSC1/CTRPv1) transfer numbers

partial_wins.statement: Any model that achieves a POSITIVE mean normalized R^2 on any one of the four external datasets under the above protocol (i.e. beats the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor in squared error on an independent screen, which no model in the public tables does; best is -0.115 on GDSC2 as of 2026-10-13), by at least 0.02 and 2x std, with the pre-registration and same-splits re-runs.
Strictly beat the live best normalized Pearson on two of the four external transfers (e.g. GDSC2 best 0.301 as of 2026-10-13) by >= 0.02 each under the same protocol.

A measured decomposition of the transfer gap: quantify, with the same splits, how much of the cross-study error is attributable to (i) drug-concentration-range differences, (ii) cell-line overlap, (iii) response-measure calibration, by re-scoring the SAME predictions after each correction, and show which single correction closes the most gap. Mechanically checkable from the written prediction CSVs, not implied by the published tables.

pitfalls: Any use of external labels - even for choosing which checkpoint, feature set or calibration to use - converts this into a fitted-on-test number. Pre-registration with a sha256-stamped config is mandatory precisely because this leak is so tempting and so invisible.

Cell-line and drug overlap between CTRPv2 and the external screens: the same cell line measured in both studies is not an independent test point in the usual sense, and silently dropping or keeping overlaps changes the number. The claim must state the overlap handling and match drevalpy's own convention.

Response-measure mismatch: GDSC lnIC50 and CTRP lnIC50 are computed from different concentration ranges and curve-fitting conventions; a naive comparison of raw MSE across studies is meaningless and an apparent win can be pure rescaling. Report both raw and per-drug-standardised metrics.

Normalized vs unnormalized metric confusion. Every public cross-study normalized R^2 is negative; quoting a positive raw R^2 (e.g. 0.223 for GradientBoosting on GDSC2) as beating the naive baseline is wrong - the naive baseline has raw R^2 0.167 and identical MSE structure.
Same-splits and same-environment re-runs are required; the attacker's pipeline version may differ from the report's, and cross-study stds are large (GradientBoosting MSE +/- 0.374).
Over-interpretation: better cross-study transfer on public cell-line screens is a benchmark result, not evidence about clinical response.

The 2025 report pages are a frozen snapshot (last modified 2025-10-17) while the maintained DrEval Challenge Leaderboard now lists 25 models, several of which are absent from the report's cross-study tables; 'no model beats the naive baseline out of study' holds only for the public cross-study tables as of the claim date. The paper itself must be read via Europe PMC, since nature.com redirects (303) a plain GET to a login host.
targets.statement: The hardest honest test in cancer drug-response prediction is transfer between independent screens. The public DrEval report includes cross-study tables: models trained on CTRPv2 under the LCO protocol are evaluated on four external datasets (GDSC1, GDSC2, CCLE, CTRPv1), and the tables are fully machine-readable Plotly tables (header: Model, MSE, RMSE, MAE, R^2, Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, and the normalized variants). As of 2026-10-13 the CTRPv2 -> GDSC2 LCO table reads (best first by MSE): GradientBoosting MSE 5.092 +/- 0.374 (normalized Pearson 0.209), RandomForest 5.095 +/- 0.139 (0.123), MultiOmicsRandomForest 5.172 (0.125), NaiveDrugMeanPredictor / NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor 5.447 +/- 0.029 (0.000), DIPK 6.407 (normalized Pearson 0.301 - the best normalized Pearson despite a worse MSE), SuperFELTR 7.919, SimpleNeuralNetwork 8.638, ElasticNet 11.775, SRMF 10880. Every model's normalized R^2 is NEGATIVE (best -0.115), i.e. no model in the public cross-study tables as of the claim date beats the naive mean-effects model on external data in squared-error terms (the newer models on the maintained DrEval Challenge Leaderboard, https://drevalpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/leaderboard.html, have no published cross-study results in the 2025 report). That is a crisp, public, currently-open frontier with a numeric table, and it is laptop-scale: training happens on CTRPv2 and scoring on an external study is a forward pass.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a drevalpy model class trained ONLY on CTRPv2 under the report's LCO protocol (package-generated splits, lnIC50, same number of CV splits) and evaluated by drevalpy's own cross-study machinery on one of the four external datasets, achieving EITHER (a) a mean MSE strictly LOWER than the minimum MSE over all models in that dataset's live cross-study table, re-fetched and re-parsed live immediately before claiming, by at least 0.10 absolute AND at least 2x the attacker's across-split std, with normalized Pearson not below the live best by more than 0.02; OR (b) a mean normalized R^2 strictly HIGHER than the live maximum in that table by at least 0.03 absolute and at least 2x the attacker's std. In both cases the attacker must include a same-environment, same-splits re-run of GradientBoosting, RandomForest and the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor and must beat the re-run values as well as the published ones. The external dataset must be used only for evaluation: no external labels, no external response statistics, no external-fitted preprocessing, and no selection of the attacker's model or hyperparameters using any external-dataset metric (choose on CTRPv2 inner validation only, and declare the chosen configuration before the external evaluation is run - the agent must log a pre-registration file with sha256 before scoring). Before claiming, the agent must also re-fetch the maintained DrEval Challenge Leaderboard (https://drevalpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/leaderboard.html) and the drevalpy repository, and check whether any newer model there has published cross-study results for the same external dataset; if so, those values are part of the bar. A result that beats only the frozen 2025 report tables while trailing a newer published cross-study value is NOT a win.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs pinned drevalpy, runs the attacker's model and the baselines with the attacker's exact invocation including --cross_study_datasets (laptop-hours to about a day), then recomputes MSE and the normalized metrics directly from drevalpy's written per-split prediction/ground-truth CSVs with their own script, including the normalisation against the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor. Record side: curl the cross-study table HTML, extract the Plotly table JSON and read the header/cells arrays (plain strings, no decoding needed). Pre-registration check: verify the sha256-stamped configuration file predates the external evaluation logs. Leakage audit: grep for any read of the external dataset during training or model selection, confirm cell lines and drugs shared between CTRPv2 and the external set are handled exactly as drevalpy's cross-study code does, and confirm no response-scale calibration was fitted on external labels.

angles: Conventional: predict ranks or per-drug standardised responses rather than absolute lnIC50, so the model never has to transport a scale across assay platforms, and map back using training-study statistics only.

Conventional: restrict to mechanistically transferable features - pathway activities, target-gene expression, known AML dependencies - instead of generic landmark genes, and let the model fall back to the mean-effects prediction where the applicability domain is violated.

Cross-domain import (signal processing / blind equalisation): treat the ex vivo screen as the same signal through a different measurement channel and estimate the channel from UNLABELLED ex vivo features only (quantile matching on the omics, not on responses), which is legitimate transduction rather than fitting on the test labels.

Cross-domain import (domain adaptation geometry / kernel mean matching): reweight CTRPv2 cell lines by an importance ratio estimated from the leading eigen-directions of the omics covariance to resemble the patient samples, which is the principled form of 'train on the cell lines that look like AML blasts'.

Cross-domain import (clinical epidemiology / transportability): borrow the formal transportability framework used to carry trial effects to new populations, which tells you in advance which effects are identifiable under a stated covariate shift and which are not - a published negative identifiability result would itself be informative here.

Cross-domain import (ecology / community similarity): compare the drug-response profile of a patient sample with training cell lines as community-composition profiles and transfer only ordinal structure, which survives effort and platform differences better than absolute values.

Honest ceiling estimation: estimate the replicate-level noise floor of BeatAML2 responses and report how much of the remaining gap is in principle reachable, which is valuable whether or not the bar is cleared.
targets.name: DrEval ex vivo transfer: beat the naive baseline when a cell-line drug-response model meets AML patient samples and breast-cancer PDX

partial_wins.statement: Strictly positive normalized Pearson and Spearman on BeatAML2 that exceed the attacker's re-run baselines (RandomForest, GradientBoosting, DIPK, NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor) by >= 0.03 each, even if normalized R-squared stays negative. Rank transfer to patient samples is a distinct and useful result.
The same criterion on PDX_Bruna, which is smaller (about 1,500 responses) and profiled on microarrays rather than RNA-seq, so a win there additionally demonstrates robustness to platform change.

A measured decomposition of the ex vivo gap: with the same predictions, quantify how much of the error is attributable to (i) assay and readout differences, (ii) expression-platform shift, (iii) the drug overlap between CTRPv2 and the ex vivo screen, by re-scoring after each correction estimated from unlabelled ex vivo features only, and report which single factor dominates. Checkable from saved prediction files; a diagnostic result, not a record.

pitfalls: Any use of ex vivo responses - for calibration, checkpoint choice, feature scaling or 'validation' - turns this into a fitted-on-test number. The sha256-stamped pre-registration and the leakage grep are the only defences, and the skeptic must check timestamps rather than trust a claim of blindness.

Drug and sample overlap: drugs shared between CTRPv2 and BeatAML2 are not independent test points in the usual sense, and silently dropping or keeping them changes the number. The overlap handling must match the package's convention and be stated.

Readout mismatch: BeatAML2 and PDX_Bruna use different viability assays, concentration ranges and curve-fitting conventions from CTRPv2, so raw squared-error comparisons across studies are meaningless; report both raw and per-drug-standardised metrics.

Normalized versus unnormalized metric confusion: a raw Pearson can look impressive while the normalized metric - the only one that measures differential sensitivity beyond mean drug and sample effects - is negative. Only the normalized metric counts here.
Subsetting: evaluating on a favourable subset of drugs, samples or splits while comparing against whole-dataset numbers, or quietly discarding samples with extreme responses.

Over-claiming is especially dangerous on this target: a positive normalized R-squared on ex vivo AML samples would be a genuine first, but it is still a retrospective laboratory measurement, not evidence that any patient should receive any drug.
targets.statement: Every cancer drug-response model is trained on immortalised cell lines and justified by an implicit promise about patient material. DrEval (Judith Bernett, Pascal Iversen, Mario Picciani, Mathias Wilhelm, Katharina Baum and Markus List; Nature Communications 2026, article 4238; package drevalpy v1.6.0) is the first benchmark to test that promise mechanically: models trained on CTRPv2 cell lines are applied, through the package's own cross-study machinery, to two ex vivo screens - BeatAML2 (about 22,500 drug-sample responses from acute myeloid leukaemia patient samples with RNA-seq) and PDX_Bruna (about 1,500 responses from breast-cancer patient-derived xenografts with microarray profiles). The paper's finding, re-read on 2026-10-15 from the open-access full text, is blunt: performance declines even more substantially on these clinically realistic datasets than in cell-line-to-cell-line transfer, where no model already beats the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor in squared error. So the open question has a crisp public form - can any model, trained only on cell lines, achieve a positive normalized R-squared (that is, beat the naive mean-effects predictor) on patient-derived material? Everything needed is ungated: the processed response and omics data on Zenodo (record 23159774, 2026-10-05: BeatAML2.zip 162 MB, PDX_Bruna.zip 50 MB, CTRPv2.zip 519 MB, splits.zip 41 MB), the package, the baselines and the metric code. This is the most clinically meaningful cell in the whole drug-response family and nobody has publicly cleared the lowest possible bar on it.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a drevalpy model class, trained ONLY on CTRPv2 under the package's documented protocol with the package-generated or Zenodo-provided splits (lnIC50, the same number of cross-validation splits as the public report), evaluated by drevalpy's own cross-study machinery on BeatAML2 (or PDX_Bruna), whose mean normalized R-squared across splits - computed by drevalpy's own evaluation code against the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor - is STRICTLY GREATER THAN ZERO (direction: max) by at least 0.02 absolute and at least 2x the across-split standard deviation, while its normalized Pearson is not lower than the attacker's same-environment re-runs of RandomForest, GradientBoosting and DIPK. The ex vivo dataset must be used for evaluation only: no response value, response statistic, calibration factor or preprocessing parameter may be derived from it, and the attacker's model and hyperparameters must be fixed on CTRPv2 inner validation and pre-registered in a sha256-stamped file written before any ex vivo scoring. Deliverables: pinned drevalpy version and commit, data sha256s, the pre-registration file with its timestamp, the model source and exact invocation, per-split prediction and ground-truth CSVs, and the same-environment baseline re-runs.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs pinned drevalpy in a clean virtual environment, downloads CTRPv2, BeatAML2 (or PDX_Bruna), meta and splits from the Zenodo record without registration and compares sha256s with the attacker's manifest, re-runs the attacker's exact invocation including the cross-study evaluation (laptop-hours to a few days on a multi-core laptop), then recomputes normalized R-squared, Pearson and Spearman directly from the written per-split prediction and ground-truth CSVs with their own script, normalising against the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor predictions that the pipeline always produces. The paper's claim that performance collapses on ex vivo data is re-read live from the Europe PMC full text. Leakage audit: verify the pre-registration file predates the ex vivo logs, grep for any read of ex vivo responses during training or model selection, and confirm no scaler, quantile map or calibration was fitted on ex vivo labels.

angles: Conventional: the normalized metric isolates differential sensitivity, so model the RESIDUAL after the mean-effects fit directly (per-drug residual regression on cell-line omics), instead of predicting lnIC50 and hoping the normalisation is kind. Per-drug residual models with heavy regularisation are the natural shape for LCO.

Conventional: better feature selection for unseen cell lines - pathway-level aggregation, variance-stabilised expression, and per-drug target-pathway priors; the published Random Forest uses generic landmark-gene features and is unlikely to be feature-optimal.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / random matrix theory): denoise the cell-line expression matrix by Marchenko-Pastur eigenvalue shrinkage before regression, keeping only components outside the bulk spectrum. LCO fails mainly because of covariate shift in noisy high-dimensional omics, which is exactly what spectral shrinkage addresses, and it costs seconds on a laptop.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / error-correcting output codes): decompose the per-drug prediction task into an ensemble of binary 'sensitive vs resistant' codewords over drug clusters and decode the cell line's response profile with a minimum-distance decoder; this turns a hard regression into many easy classifications and recovers rank signal (Pearson/Spearman normalized) that the regression loss throws away.

Cross-domain import (ecology / community similarity): treat cell lines as 'sites' and drugs as 'species' and import beta-diversity / ordination machinery (Procrustes alignment of drug-response ordinations between training and held-out cell lines) to transfer response geometry rather than point predictions.

Variance reduction and honest tuning: because the bar is 0.02 normalized R^2, ensembling across splits, bagged feature subsets and careful inner-validation-only tuning may matter as much as the model class; measure the across-split standard error first and refuse to chase gains below it.
targets.name: DrEval leave-cell-line-out: beat the public best normalized R^2 / Pearson for cancer drug-response prediction on CTRPv2

partial_wins.statement: Same criterion in the LTO (leave-tissue-out) setting against https://dilis-lab.github.io/drevalpy-report/heatmaps/heatmap_algorithms_LTO_normalized.html (live best normalized R^2 as of 2026-10-13: 0.0728, RandomForest), by >= 0.02 absolute, with the same same-splits re-run requirement.

Strictly beat the live best normalized Pearson (0.4347 as of 2026-10-13) and normalized Spearman (0.4283) in LCO by >= 0.01 each while not losing more than 0.01 of normalized R^2 relative to the live best. Rank-correlation gains without R^2 gains are a separate, independently checkable result.

A negative result of record: a same-environment, same-splits re-run of the published RandomForest, MultiOmicsRandomForest and DIPK in LCO showing a reproducibility gap of > 0.02 normalized R^2 against the published report values, with full logs. This is a reproducibility finding about the public benchmark, not a win, and must be reported as such.

pitfalls: Same-splits comparison is mandatory. drevalpy regenerates CV splits; comparing a local run against the published report numbers without re-running the Random Forest baseline in the same environment and splits is the single most likely false positive here, because split variance in LCO is large relative to the 0.02 bar.

Normalisation confusion: 'normalized R^2' is relative to the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor, and unnormalized R^2 can look spectacular (LPO overall Pearson ~0.91 for DIPK) while carrying zero differential-sensitivity signal. Quoting an unnormalized number as a record is the classic crank move in this field.

Cell-line identity leakage through omics preprocessing: fitting scalers, PCA, gene filters, batch correction or drug/cell-line embeddings on the full dataset before splitting lets held-out cell lines inform training. LCO specifically forbids this, and it is invisible in the output metrics.
Response-measure substitution: the public run predicts lnIC50. Switching to AUC or pEC50, or to GDSC instead of CTRPv2, changes the achievable numbers entirely and is not a comparable record.

Cross-study confusion: the report also contains cross-study tables (CTRPv2 -> GDSC2 etc.) with different and lower values; comparing an in-study result against a cross-study table (or vice versa) invalidates the claim.
Duplicate drug-cell-line pairs and replicate rows in CTRPv2 straddling folds; drevalpy handles this for its own splits, but any custom data joining by the attacker can reintroduce it.

Two different public scoreboards exist for CTRPv2 LCO: the 2025 report heatmaps (frozen, last modified 2025-10-17, 11-15 models, the package's own 10-fold run) and the maintained DrEval Challenge Leaderboard (precomputed splits from Zenodo splits.zip, LN_IC50_curvecurator, 25 models as of 2026-10-15). They are not comparable to each other, and beating the older one is not a record.
targets.statement: DrEval (drevalpy, Bernett et al., Nature Communications 2026, article 4238) is a standardised benchmark for drug-response prediction in cancer cell lines. Its headline finding is that complex deep models barely beat a naive predictor of mean drug and cell-line effects, and that NO published model surpasses a tuned Random Forest in the leave-cell-line-out (LCO) setting. The full public benchmark report is served as static HTML at https://dilis-lab.github.io/drevalpy-report/ (run id all_runs; the documented main run is CTRPv2 lnIC50 with 10-fold CV and cross-study evaluation on CTRPv1/CCLE/GDSC1/GDSC2, test modes LPO/LCO/LTO/LDO). The per-model metric table is machine-readable: heatmaps/heatmap_algorithms_LCO_normalized.html embeds a Plotly figure whose z values are base64 float64 arrays. As of 2026-10-13 the LCO ranking by normalized R^2 is RandomForest 0.1852, MultiOmicsRandomForest 0.1633, ProteomicsRandomForest 0.1612, DIPK 0.1084, SimpleNeuralNetwork 0.0706, GradientBoosting 0.0545, MultiOmicsNeuralNetwork 0.0003, naive baselines ~ -0.002 and below; by normalized Pearson, RandomForest 0.4347 leads. 'Normalized' means after subtracting the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor, i.e. the metric measures only the differential-sensitivity signal, which is where every method is still weak (the paper notes all models stay below 0.20 normalized R^2 in LCO). Beating a tuned Random Forest on this normalized metric with CPU-only methods is a genuine, narrow, currently-open frontier, and drevalpy runs end-to-end on a laptop (the pipeline, splits, baselines and metrics all ship in the package, v1.6.0 archived on Zenodo, repo pushed 2026-10-13).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a new model, implemented as a drevalpy model class, run through drevalpy's own pipeline on the same dataset and test mode as the public report (CTRPv2, test_mode=LCO, the same number of CV splits as the report's run, lnIC50 response, the package's own split generation with the report's seed/configuration), whose mean normalized R^2 across the CV splits, computed by drevalpy's own evaluation code, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum normalized R^2 over ALL models in https://dilis-lab.github.io/drevalpy-report/heatmaps/heatmap_algorithms_LCO_normalized.html, re-fetched and re-decoded live immediately before claiming, by at least 0.02 absolute AND by at least 2x the across-split standard error of the attacker's own result, while not being worse than the live best normalized Pearson by more than 0.01. The claim must ship: pinned drevalpy version and commit, the model class source, the exact CLI/API invocation, the per-split predictions and ground-truth CSVs that drevalpy writes, the drevalpy-generated report directory, and a re-run of the published RandomForest baseline in the SAME environment and splits (so the comparison is same-splits, not report-vs-local). If the attacker's own RandomForest re-run differs from the published 0.1852 by more than 0.02, the comparison must be made against the attacker's own re-run AND against the published value, and both must be beaten. Hyperparameters may be selected only with the inner validation partitions drevalpy provides; no test fold may be touched before the final evaluation. In addition, before claiming, the agent must re-fetch the maintained DrEval Challenge Leaderboard (https://drevalpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/leaderboard.html and the rendered leaderboard image in the drevalpy repository, which as of 2026-10-15 lists 25 models on CTRPv2 LCO with best normalized Pearson 0.376 (EnsembleMF) and best RMSE 1.274 (DrugGNN)) and must show that its normalized Pearson is not lower than the live leaderboard maximum. A result that beats only the frozen 2025 report heatmap, while trailing a model already on the live leaderboard, is NOT a win and must be reported as a reproduction-scale result.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs the pinned drevalpy in a clean venv, runs the attacker's model class plus the RandomForest baseline on CTRPv2 LCO with the attacker's exact invocation (drevalpy writes per-split predictions, ground truth and metrics as CSVs; laptop-hours to about a day on 10 cores), then recomputes normalized R^2 directly from the CSVs with their own script (normalization against the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor predictions, which the pipeline always produces), and confirms the drevalpy-reported value matches. Record side: curl the table_url, extract the Plotly JSON, base64-decode the z array, and read the live maximum. Leakage audit: confirm the test folds' cell lines never appear in training for that split, that no omics preprocessing (feature selection, scaling, PCA, gene filtering) was fitted on all cell lines jointly, and that no hyperparameter was chosen using test-fold predictions.

angles: Conventional: predict the drug's RESPONSE PROFILE across cell lines as a whole object (a vector), from structure and target annotations, rather than predicting scalar responses one pair at a time; nearest-profile retrieval over training drugs with a learned structural metric is the strongest classical approach to unseen-compound transfer.

Conventional: mechanism-of-action features instead of raw fingerprints - target gene sets, pathway membership, and the correlation of the drug's nominal targets with cell-line dependency/expression - plus a mean-effects baseline the model only has to correct.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / nearest-neighbour decoding): treat each training drug's response profile as a codeword and the unseen drug's structural features as a noisy channel output, then decode by minimum-distance over a learned metric with soft-decision weighting; this is exactly a list-decoding problem and brings principled confidence estimates that let the model abstain on drugs with no structural neighbour (abstention is allowed to improve correlation metrics only if it is applied uniformly and reported).

Cross-domain import (compression / normalised compression distance): define drug-drug similarity by the compressibility of concatenated SMILES / target-set descriptions (NCD) rather than by hand-chosen fingerprints, and use it as the kernel in a Gaussian-process or kernel-ridge model; parameter-free similarity measures often beat tuned fingerprints in the extreme-extrapolation regime and cost nothing on a laptop.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics): fit a low-rank-plus-sparse factorisation of the drug x cell-line response matrix with a replica-style regularisation path, then map new drugs into the latent drug space by structural regression; the question of how much of the latent space is structurally predictable is itself a measurable, reportable quantity.

Honest ceiling estimation: estimate the irreducible noise floor from replicate drugs and near-duplicate compounds in CTRPv2 and report how much of the remaining gap is in principle reachable; this is useful whether or not the record falls.
targets.name: DrEval leave-drug-out: the open question of beating the naive mean-effects baseline for unseen cancer drugs

partial_wins.statement: Strictly beat the live best LDO normalized Spearman (0.3559 as of 2026-10-13) and normalized Pearson (0.3538) by >= 0.01 each under the same protocol, without being worse than the live best normalized R^2 by more than 0.01. Rank transfer to unseen drugs is a distinct, checkable result.

A mechanically documented impossibility-style result instead of a win: show, with the same splits and 20+ model/feature configurations (including structure fingerprints, target annotations, and a mean-effects-plus-residual family), that none exceeds normalized R^2 0.02 in LDO, and provide a per-drug analysis identifying which drug classes carry what little transferable signal exists. Must be reported as a negative benchmark result with all runs logged, and is non-trivial because the public report covers only ~11 models.

A same-splits reproducibility check of the published LDO ordering: show that the published ordering of the top three LDO models by normalized R^2 is or is not stable across two independent split generations, with full logs. Independently checkable and not implied by the published report, which reports one split generation.

pitfalls: Per-drug statistic leakage is the dominant trap: any per-drug mean, median, rank, scaling factor or embedding computed on the full dataset gives the model the held-out drugs' response level, which is nearly the whole metric in LDO. A model that looks like it 'learned chemistry' is usually just reading a leaked per-drug mean.

Near-duplicate compounds: CTRPv2 contains structurally near-identical drugs and multiple salts/analogues of the same scaffold. If a test drug's analogue sits in training, the result generalises to nothing. The skeptic must report maximum Tanimoto similarity between each test drug and the training set and show the gain is not confined to high-similarity drugs.

Same-splits comparison: the LDO numbers are small and split variance is large, so comparing a local run against published report values without re-running the baselines in the same splits and environment will manufacture a fake record. Two independent split generations are required here.
Metric swap: unnormalized R^2 in LDO is dominated by the mean-effects structure and can be positive while normalized R^2 is negative. Only the normalized metric, as drevalpy computes it, counts.
Abstention or subsetting: dropping hard test drugs, filtering to a drug class, or evaluating on a subset of folds while comparing against full-benchmark numbers.
Over-claiming: a normalized R^2 of 0.05 for unseen drugs is a benchmark result about a public cell-line screen, not a statement about which drug to give anyone. The write-up must say so.
targets.statement: In DrEval's leave-drug-out (LDO) setting - predict responses for drugs never seen in training - the published benchmark reports that essentially NO model meaningfully beats the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor: normalized R^2 is approximately zero for every method. The live public report confirms it: in https://dilis-lab.github.io/drevalpy-report/heatmaps/heatmap_algorithms_LDO_normalized.html the normalized R^2 ranking as of 2026-10-13 is MultiOmicsNeuralNetwork 0.0235, GradientBoosting 0.0108, SimpleNeuralNetwork -0.0105, NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor -0.0169, DIPK -0.0181, ElasticNet -0.0305, ProteomicsRandomForest -0.0401, MultiOmicsRandomForest -0.0416, NaiveTissueMeanPredictor -0.0605, NaivePredictor -0.0892, RandomForest -0.1186; the normalized rank metrics are more forgiving (DIPK leads with normalized Spearman 0.3559, Pearson 0.3538). So the frontier is stark and public: generalising to unseen compounds from chemical structure is the unsolved half of cancer drug-response prediction, and the best published normalized R^2 is barely above zero. A laptop-scale agents can attack this because the whole pipeline, the splits, the baselines and the metric are in drevalpy, and the bar is low in absolute terms while being genuinely open.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a drevalpy model class, run through drevalpy's own pipeline on the same dataset and test mode as the public report (CTRPv2, test_mode=LDO, same number of CV splits, lnIC50 response, package-generated splits), whose mean normalized R^2 computed by drevalpy's own evaluation code is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum normalized R^2 over ALL models in https://dilis-lab.github.io/drevalpy-report/heatmaps/heatmap_algorithms_LDO_normalized.html, re-fetched and re-decoded live immediately before claiming, by at least 0.02 absolute AND by at least 2x the across-split standard error of the attacker's result, with the attacker's own same-environment same-splits re-run of BOTH the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor and the published LDO leader (MultiOmicsNeuralNetwork) included, and the attacker's value beating both. Deliverables: pinned drevalpy version/commit, model source, exact invocation, per-split prediction and ground-truth CSVs, the generated report directory, and a seed-repeat run showing the gain survives a second independent split generation. Chemical features for held-out drugs must be derived from structure/target annotations only; no information computed from the test drugs' responses (including per-drug means, ranks, or any statistic of the held-out fold) may enter the model.
targets.verification_method: As for the LCO target: clean venv, pinned drevalpy, re-run the attacker's model plus the NaiveMeanEffectsPredictor and the published LDO leader on CTRPv2 LDO with the attacker's exact invocation (laptop-hours to about a day), recompute normalized R^2 and the rank metrics directly from the written per-split CSVs with the skeptic's own script, and confirm agreement with drevalpy's output. Then curl the table_url, decode the Plotly z-array and read the live maximum. Leakage audit specific to LDO: assert the test fold's drugs appear nowhere in training (including in any precomputed drug-similarity matrix, fingerprint PCA, or drug embedding), and that per-drug statistics were never computed over the full dataset.

angles: CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing, the natural fit): treat each spectrum as a signal, not a feature vector - baseline estimation (asymmetric least squares), variance-stabilising transforms, wavelet denoising and peak deconvolution with mass-calibration alignment (dynamic time warping across spectra) before any learning; most published gains in this field came from preprocessing, not architecture.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / dictionary learning): learn a sparse dictionary of peak motifs (K-SVD / NMF) across all species, then classify in the sparse-code space; this shares statistical strength across species-drug pairs with very few positives.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / spin-glass style modelling): model peak co-occurrence as an interaction network and use its low-temperature modes as features, which captures correlated proteome runs rather than individual peaks.

Domain adaptation across hospitals: optimal-transport or CORAL-style alignment of spectra distributions between DRIAMS sites, plus per-site calibration, aimed directly at the site-transfer regime the original paper found hardest.

Label-efficiency: with few resistant isolates for some drugs, use multi-task learning across drugs of the same class, positive-unlabelled learning, and conformal prediction to get honest uncertainty; report precision-recall, not just AUROC.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology): treat the peak list as a community-composition sample (relative abundances) and import diversity/ordination statistics (Aitchison geometry, CLR transforms) designed for compositional data, which spectra effectively are.
targets.name: DRIAMS MALDI-TOF resistance prediction: beat the published per-species-drug AUROC on the public spectra

partial_wins.statement: Beat the published cross-hospital (site-transfer) AUROC for one species-drug pair by >= 0.02 with no target-site labels used in training, bootstrap interval excluding zero.

Match the published same-site AUROC to within 0.01 using only a linear model on <= 50 interpretable mass bins (peak list), with the bins named and the model released - an interpretability result, reported as such.

A reproducible confound audit: demonstrate with held-out data how much of the published performance for one species-drug pair is attributable to species/site/acquisition-batch signal rather than resistance (e.g. by label permutation within batch, batch-only predictors, and acquisition-date splits), quantified and released as code.

pitfalls: Batch and site confounding: acquisition batch, hospital and even plate position correlate with resistance prevalence, so a model can score well by learning the batch. Any claim needs batch-aware splits and the permutation/metadata-only controls, otherwise it is a false positive.
Replicate leakage: the same isolate or patient can contribute multiple spectra; random spectrum-level splits then put near-duplicates on both sides. Splits must be by isolate/patient identifier.

Species leakage: species identification is itself derivable from the spectrum, and resistance prevalence differs sharply by species; models must be evaluated within a fixed species, as the published numbers are.

AUROC on heavy imbalance: for rare resistance the AUROC can be high while precision is useless. The claim must include AUPRC and raw counts, and the comparator must be the published value for the same species-drug pair and split regime, not a different one.

Version drift: DRIAMS has been re-released multiple times (Dryad version 12 of 2025-08-19); comparing a model trained on a newer release to numbers published on an older one is apples to oranges unless the exact version and subset are matched and stated.

Dryad now serves file downloads behind a bot challenge; fetch DRIAMS from the Zenodo mirror and record which mirror and which version was used, because version numbering differs between the two hosts.
targets.statement: DRIAMS ('Database of Resistance Information on Antimicrobials and MALDI-TOF Mass Spectra', Dryad version 12 of 2025-08-19, CC0, 144 GB; mirrored on Zenodo record 5640517 as DRIAMS_A 86 GB, DRIAMS_B 3.7 GB, DRIAMS_C 12.4 GB and DRIAMS_D 42.6 GB, because Dryad's file endpoints are gated for plain downloads) is a public collection of ~300k clinical MALDI-TOF mass spectra with linked antimicrobial susceptibility labels from four hospitals, released with the Weis et al. study that predicted resistance directly from spectra and reported per-species-drug AUROC (notably for Staphylococcus aureus/oxacillin, Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae/ceftriaxone). The accompanying code is public (github.com/BorgwardtLab/maldi_amr, frozen since 2022-10-07, so there is no maintained leaderboard: the bar is the paper). A claim must state which DRIAMS site it uses; the smaller sites, or the binned_6000 spectra of one site and species-drug pair, keep it laptop-sized. Spectra are 1-D signals of a few thousand bins, so training and evaluation are minutes-to-hours on a CPU, and the published AUROCs leave real headroom - particularly for cross-hospital (site-transfer) evaluation, which the original work flags as the hard regime. Rapid resistance phenotyping from routine mass spectra is a neglected, high-leverage corner of AMR with almost no community benchmark activity.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for at least one species-antibiotic pair, a released model and saved per-spectrum predictions evaluated on a split that is defined before training and is at least as strict as the published one (same DRIAMS site, same species-drug pair, same label definition; patient/isolate identifiers never split across train and test), whose AUROC exceeds the published AUROC for that same species-drug pair and split regime (read live from the Weis et al. paper and github.com/BorgwardtLab/maldi_amr immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02 AND outside a 95% bootstrap interval over test spectra, with the number of positives/negatives, the full ROC and a precision-recall curve reported alongside. Spectra preprocessing must be the published pipeline or a documented superset applied identically to train and test, and the exact DRIAMS version and split files (sha256) must be published with the claim. A cross-site claim (train on site A, test on site B) must be compared only against published cross-site numbers.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the pinned DRIAMS version from the Zenodo mirror (record 5640517, plain HTTPS with range requests; DRIAMS-A alone is 86 GB, so fetch the declared site and use its binned_6000 spectra for the single species-drug pair claimed), verifies the attacker's split files by sha256 and checks no isolate/patient identifier appears in both train and test, reruns the attacker's released preprocessing and model to regenerate predictions, computes AUROC and AUPRC with bootstrap intervals, and re-reads the published numbers from the paper and the maldi_amr repo. Confound checks: train a predictor on acquisition metadata alone and on permuted labels within batch, and confirm the claimed signal is not reproduced.

angles: Respect the support: the target is a bounded proportion, so logit-scale modelling with heteroscedastic, horizon-dependent spread and back-transformed quantiles avoids the crossing and tail problems that cost WIS on count-style models.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / control): a state-space model on logit-proportion with a time-varying growth state and revisions treated as observation noise produces calibrated intervals without hand-tuned spread.

CROSS-DOMAIN (econometrics of mixed-frequency data): ED visits lead admissions, so a leading-indicator regression (MIDAS-style) exploits the two targets' different timing instead of modelling each in isolation.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / nonlinear dynamics): analogue forecasting across jurisdictions as replicate trajectories handles season-shape variation that parametric curves miss, especially at turning points.
Backfill first: the most recent weeks of NSSP proportions are revised, so an explicit revision model for the last two weeks is probably the largest single WIS gain.
Hierarchical pooling across jurisdictions and the two targets, with shrinkage of growth-rate volatility toward a national mean - the ensemble averages models, not information.
targets.name: CDC FluSight emergency-department visits: beat the FluSight-ensemble's season WIS on the newer ED-visit target

partial_wins.statement: Strictly lower season-average WIS than the FluSight-baseline AND than the median submitted model on the ED-visit target for one completed season, under the as-of discipline and the hub's scorer.
Beat the ensemble at horizons 2-3 weeks ahead on the ED-visit target across all locations of one completed season, reported as a horizon-restricted result.

A transfer result: show that a single model fitted jointly on the admissions and ED-visit targets beats the same model fitted on ED visits alone, by a margin with an interval, quantifying how much the older target's history is worth.

pitfalls: Look-ahead through revisions: the ED-visit series is revised after first report; fitting on the final series while claiming a retrospective forecast is the classic false positive here.
Target confusion: the hub scores two targets with different units and different reports; comparing against the hospital-admissions ensemble value, or mixing the targets' rows, invalidates the claim.
Mismatched task sets: the ensemble's published score covers specific locations, horizons and dates with exclusion rules; dropping low-volume jurisdictions is the commonest fake win.
Hindsight tuning: choosing the transform, window or spread multiplier after seeing the season's scores must be excluded by freezing parameters on earlier seasons with commit evidence.
Ensemble contamination: consuming other teams' submissions for the scored season makes the result a combination, not a forecast.
A WIS improvement is a forecasting-method result and is not public-health guidance.
targets.statement: The CDC FluSight hub added a second prediction target - the weekly proportion of emergency-department visits attributed to influenza, from the National Syndromic Surveillance Program - alongside its long-running hospital-admissions target, and publishes a separate end-of-season evaluation for it (reports/'Flu_ED_Visit_Forecasts_WIS_27 May 2026.html' in github.com/cdcepi/FluSight-forecast-hub, directory fetched 2026-10-15; model-output holds every team's submissions through 2026-10-17, and target-data holds oracle-output.csv, 17 MB, plus the 89 MB time-series.csv with as-of values). The ED-visit target is young: fewer teams have tuned models for a bounded proportion with its own reporting artefacts, the series is revised, and the ensemble's lead over the baseline is correspondingly less entrenched than on admissions. The scoring rule is the open hubverse weighted interval score, so a stranger can rescore everything on a laptop.
targets.success_criterion: Success means saved quantile forecasts, in the hub's submission format for the ED-visit target, covering every reference date, location and horizon of ONE completed season for which FluSight-ensemble submitted, produced by a released deterministic pipeline that at each reference date uses only data available then (the hub's as-of target data or an archived snapshot; no final revised series, no oracle-output, no other team's submissions, no parameter tuned on later weeks of that season), whose season-average WIS, computed with public hubverse scoring code against the hub's oracle-output for that season under the hub's exclusion rules, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the FluSight-ensemble's for the same target, season, locations, horizons and reference dates as published in the hub's ED-visit evaluation report in https://github.com/cdcepi/FluSight-forecast-hub/tree/main/reports , re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 3% relative AND outside a stationary-bootstrap 90% interval over reference dates. The scorer must first reproduce the ensemble's published value for that season to within 1%.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the hub at a pinned commit, validates the attacker's files against hub-config task-ids for the ED-visit target, recomputes WIS for the attacker, the ensemble and the baseline with public hubverse code (first reproducing the published report value), bootstraps over reference dates, and audits look-ahead by rerunning the pipeline on truncated snapshots and by grepping for reads of oracle-output, of future weeks or of model-output. Under a gigabyte, CPU-only.

angles: Distributional discipline first: WIS rewards calibration more than point accuracy. Fit a simple, robust mean model (seasonal climatology plus recent trend) and spend the effort on the predictive distribution: quantile regression with heteroscedastic, horizon-dependent spread, conformalised quantiles from past residuals, and tail widening when the trend reverses.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / control theory): treat weekly admissions as a noisy signal and forecast with a state-space model (Kalman/particle filter on log-incidence with a time-varying growth-rate state), which naturally produces calibrated intervals and handles reporting revisions as observation noise; add a Savitzky-Golay or wavelet denoiser before trend extraction.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / renewal theory): model epidemic growth as a renewal process with a time-varying reproduction number driven by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, and propagate parameter uncertainty analytically; this is the physics-style answer to overconfident curve fits.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology): borrow empirical-dynamic-modelling/nonlinear-time-series tools (simplex projection, S-map, attractor reconstruction across the 50+ state time series as a spatial replicate ensemble) to forecast by nearest-neighbour analogues of past season trajectories instead of parametric curves.

Hierarchical pooling across locations and seasons: partial pooling (empirical Bayes shrinkage of growth rates toward national and census-division means) is where small-state WIS is won; the ensemble averages models, not information, so a properly pooled single model can beat it.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / MDL for model selection): choose among candidate forecast families online by prequential (predictive) code length rather than by in-sample fit, which is exactly a WIS-friendly log-loss analogue and avoids the hindsight tuning that makes retrospective wins fake.

Exploit documented ensemble weaknesses: turning points, holiday-week reporting artefacts, and seasons with early onset; a model that handles reporting-delay backfill explicitly (nowcast the most recent 2 weeks before forecasting) attacks the ensemble where it is structurally weak.
targets.name: CDC FluSight hub: beat the FluSight-ensemble's season-average WIS retrospectively on a completed season

partial_wins.statement: Strictly lower season-average WIS than the FluSight-baseline model AND than the median submitted model for the same season/target/locations, under the same as-of data discipline and the hub's scorer, with the bootstrap interval excluding zero.

Beat the FluSight-ensemble's WIS on the subset of forecasts at horizons 2-3 weeks ahead (where the ensemble is weakest) for all locations in a completed season, with the official scorer and the no-look-ahead audit, reported as a horizon-restricted result.

A reproducible scoring audit: independently recompute the hub's published per-model season WIS table for a completed season from model-output/ plus oracle-output.csv with hubverse code, and document any model whose recomputed WIS differs from the published value by more than 1%, with the cause (missing submissions, revised targets, exclusion rules).

pitfalls: Look-ahead/backfill leakage: hospitalisation and ED-visit targets are revised for weeks after first report. Training or fitting on the FINAL time series while claiming a retrospective forecast is the classic false positive here; only as-of snapshots (or the hub's versioned target data) may be used, and the oracle-output must never be read by the pipeline.

Hindsight tuning: picking the model class, window length, or spread multiplier after seeing which choice scores best on that season is overfitting dressed as forecasting. Hyperparameters must be fixed on earlier seasons and frozen, with the commit history or a pre-registration to show it.

Mismatched comparison sets: the ensemble's published WIS covers specific reference dates, locations, horizons and target (hospital admissions vs ED visits), with hub exclusion rules for missing or invalid submissions. Scoring the attacker on an easier subset (e.g. dropping low-count jurisdictions or a bad month) is the commonest way to fake a win.

Scoring-rule errors: WIS must use the hub's exact quantile levels, with counts not rates, non-crossing quantiles, and the same log/natural scale as the official report; an averaging order change (mean of per-location WIS vs pooled) can move results by more than the claimed margin.
Ensemble contamination: using other teams' submitted forecasts, or an ensemble member's output, for the same season turns the result into a post-hoc combination rather than a forecaster.
targets.statement: The CDC FluSight forecast hub (github.com/cdcepi/FluSight-forecast-hub) stores every weekly probabilistic forecast ever submitted by every team (model-output/, one parquet/csv per model per reference date), the ground-truth target data including a hubverse oracle-output.csv (17 MB, fetched 2026-10-13) and time-series.csv (88 MB), the ensemble weights, and the official weighted-interval-score (WIS) evaluation reports (reports/Flu_Hospitalizations_Forecasts_WIS_27 May 2026.html and Flu_ED_Visit_Forecasts_WIS_27 May 2026.html, i.e. the 2025-26 season's end-of-season evaluation). The FluSight-ensemble routinely ranks at or near the top and beating it out-of-sample is a standing open problem in epidemic forecasting. Everything needed to score a new forecaster against every submitted model on a frozen, completed season is public, small and CPU-only, and the scoring rule (WIS over the hub's quantile levels, per horizon/location/target) is implemented in the open hubverse packages.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released, deterministic forecasting pipeline plus saved quantile forecasts that (a) cover every reference date, location and horizon of ONE completed FluSight season as submitted-format output matching the hub's task-id schema in hub-config/, (b) at each reference date use ONLY data that was available on that date (the pipeline must read from the hub's own versioned/as-of target data or an archived data snapshot, and the code must be auditable for look-ahead, including no parameters tuned on later weeks of the same season), and (c) achieve a season-average WIS, computed with the public hubverse scoring code on the hub's oracle-output.csv for that season with the hub's own exclusion rules, STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the FluSight-ensemble's season-average WIS for the same target, horizons, locations and reference dates as published in the hub's evaluation report in https://github.com/cdcepi/FluSight-forecast-hub/tree/main/reports , re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 2% relative AND outside a stationary-bootstrap 90% interval over reference dates. A forecaster that consumes any other model's submitted forecasts for that season (including the ensemble's) is disqualified.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the hub at a pinned commit (model-output/, target-data/oracle-output.csv, hub-config/, reports/), validates the attacker's forecast files against the hub's validation schema, recomputes WIS for the attacker and for FluSight-ensemble/FluSight-baseline with the public hubverse scoring code (R hubEvals or an equivalent re-implementation cross-checked on the published numbers), and bootstraps over reference dates. Look-ahead audit: rerun the attacker's pipeline with the data snapshot truncated at each reference date and confirm the forecasts are reproduced bit-for-bit (or within documented stochastic tolerance), and grep the code and configs for any read of future weeks, of oracle-output.csv, or of other teams' submissions. All data is well under 1 GB.

angles: Model the delay distribution properly: a hierarchical negative-binomial delay model with day-of-week effects, state and age-group random effects and a slowly varying reporting-probability curve is the textbook nowcast and still beats most submissions when fitted carefully.

CROSS-DOMAIN (survival analysis): the reporting triangle is right-truncated survival data, so inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting and discrete-time hazard models transfer directly and give calibrated intervals.

CROSS-DOMAIN (queueing theory): treat reports as arrivals through a server with time-varying capacity (weekends, holidays, backlog clearance) rather than as a static delay distribution - backlog dynamics are exactly what breaks naive nowcasts.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / deconvolution): nowcasting is deconvolution of a known-ish delay kernel from a truncated signal; regularised Richardson-Lucy or total-variation deconvolution with uncertainty by bootstrap is an unexploited angle.
Borrow strength across strata: states and age groups share delay structure; partial pooling plus post-stratification stabilises the thin strata where the ensemble is weakest.
Calibration last: conformalise the predictive quantiles on past nowcast errors, since WIS rewards honest spread far more than a better point estimate.
targets.name: German COVID-19 hospitalization nowcast hub: beat the hub ensemble's WIS on the published real-time nowcasts

partial_wins.statement: Beat the ensemble by >= 5% relative WIS restricted to the youngest and oldest age strata, where delays are longest and the submitted pool thinnest, over the declared period.
Beat every individual submitted model (not necessarily the ensemble) over the declared period under the as-of discipline, with the bootstrap interval excluding zero.

A reproduction of the hub's published evaluation: recompute per-model WIS for the published period from data-processed and the truth data with a released script, documenting every discrepancy and the exclusion rules needed to reconcile it.

pitfalls: Triangle leakage: using the completed truth for past dates instead of the triangle as it stood is the defining false positive of nowcasting work; the audit must rerun the pipeline on truncated triangles.
Revision definition: the RKI series was itself revised and redefined during the period; the claim must state which truth version it scores against and use the same one for both predictors.
Row mismatch across strata: the ensemble does not cover every state/age/date cell; scoring on an easier subset is the commonest way to fake a win.
Short evaluation windows: the hub's window is limited, so a few weeks of luck can look like skill; the stationary bootstrap over dates and a minimum window length are required.
Consuming other teams' nowcasts turns the result into a post-hoc combination rather than a nowcaster.
A WIS improvement on an archived German series is a methods result, not public-health guidance.
targets.statement: Nowcasting - estimating today's value of a statistic that will only be complete in weeks - is the neglected half of epidemic forecasting, and Germany's seven-day COVID-19 hospitalization incidence was a textbook case because reports arrive with long, age- and state-dependent delays. The Hospitalization Nowcast Hub run by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology chair of econometrics and statistics with the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies (github.com/KITmetricslab/hospitalization-nowcast-hub) archives, in a standard format, every submitted real-time nowcast (data-processed), retrospective nowcasts (data-processed_retrospective), and the Robert Koch Institute truth data with its full reporting triangle (data-truth). Daniel Wolffram, Johannes Bracher and colleagues published the collaborative evaluation in 2023 (PMC10446237), scoring models and the ensemble by weighted interval score across states and age groups. The data is tens of megabytes and the whole exercise is CPU-only.
targets.success_criterion: Success means saved quantile nowcasts, in the hub's submission format, for every (forecast_date, location, age_group, delay horizon) row for which the hub ensemble has a nowcast over one declared continuous evaluation period of at least eight weeks within the hub's operating window, produced by a deterministic pipeline that at each date reads ONLY the reporting triangle as it stood on that date (the hub's dated truth files), whose mean weighted interval score against the hub's final truth, recomputed by the skeptic with public scoring code on exactly those rows, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the ensemble's by at least 5% relative, with a stationary bootstrap over dates at 90% excluding zero. The scorer must first reproduce the ensemble's published scores from https://github.com/KITmetricslab/hospitalization-nowcast-hub and the evaluation of https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10446237/fullTextXML (re-read live immediately before claiming) to within 1%. Submitted nowcasts of other teams may not be consumed.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the hub at a pinned commit, reconstructs the reporting triangle as of each nowcast date from the dated truth files, validates the attacker's files against the hub format, recomputes WIS for the attacker and the ensemble on identical rows with public code (validated by reproducing the published numbers), bootstraps over dates, and audits for look-ahead by rerunning the pipeline on truncated triangles and by code review. Tens of megabytes, minutes of CPU.

angles: Conventional: replace ridge-on-PCA with a head that matches the data's structure - per-gene shrinkage toward the slide mean, multi-output reduced-rank regression, or a Poisson/negative-binomial likelihood on counts instead of Gaussian regression on normalised values.

Conventional: use the spatial arrangement the published pipeline throws away - neighbourhood averaging of embeddings, conditional autoregressive smoothing of predictions, or multi-scale patches - while keeping the train/test patient split intact.

Cross-domain import (signal processing / super-resolution): expression over a slide is a smooth field sampled on a lattice; borrow deconvolution and total-variation denoising from image restoration to separate the measurable low-frequency field from per-spot shot noise, and predict only the part that is predictable.

Cross-domain import (geostatistics / kriging): this is literally a spatial prediction problem with a known covariance structure; fit a variogram per gene per slide and use kriging with the image embedding as external drift, which is the standard tool in mining and soil science for exactly this data shape.

Cross-domain import (ecology / rarefaction): spot-level counts differ in sequencing depth exactly as ecological surveys differ in effort; coverage-based rarefaction per spot before correlating removes a nuisance axis that currently inflates variance in the weak tasks.

Cross-domain import (compression / MDL): choose the number of PCA factors and the per-gene regularisation by description length rather than validation Pearson; with only a handful of patients per task, validation-based selection is itself extremely noisy.

Ensembling encoders: the table shows 25 encoders whose errors are probably decorrelated; a rank- or precision-weighted ensemble of two or three embeddings, with weights fitted on training patients only, is cheap and untested in the published table.
targets.name: HEST-Benchmark: beat the best published Pearson for predicting spatial gene expression from tumour histology

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live best on two of the three weakest tasks (as of 2026-10-15: READ 0.2421, CCRCC 0.2719, LYMPH_IDC 0.2842) by >= 0.015 each with ONE frozen configuration, which is far stronger evidence than a single-task win on the easy IDC or SKCM tasks.

Show that a non-foundation-model pipeline (stains-normalised classical texture/colour features, or a small CPU-trainable encoder) exceeds the published ResNet50 average of 0.3252 by >= 0.03 on at least four tasks, quantifying how much of the foundation-model advantage is reproducible without a large pretrained encoder.

A spatial-leakage audit: re-score the published-style ridge pipeline after enforcing a minimum physical distance between training and test spots within the same slide, and report how much of the reported Pearson on each task is attributable to neighbouring-spot correlation. A benchmark-critique result, checkable from the saved spot coordinates and predictions.

pitfalls: Spot-level leakage within a slide: patches from the same tumour region are strongly correlated, so any split that is not strictly by patient/sample, or any smoothing that crosses the train/test boundary, manufactures correlation. Verify the split files are used exactly as published.

Metric definition drift: the published numbers are Pearson per gene averaged in a specific way after a specific normalisation (ridge on PCA-256 embeddings). Recomputing with a different gene set, different normalisation or a different averaging order moves the number by more than the 0.015 bar.

Encoder provenance and training-data contamination: several listed encoders were pretrained on public cohorts that may overlap HEST slides. A claim built on a new pretrained encoder must state its pretraining corpus; otherwise an apparent win can be memorisation of the same slides.
Single-seed and single-task cherry-picking: with few patients per task, seed and split variance is large. Five seeds, a 2x-std margin and a full nine-task report are required.
Stale-table comparison: the README table has been updated repeatedly (entries dated 30.08.24 and 03.04.26) and accepts community pull requests, so the record must be re-read live before claiming.

Over-claiming: predicting 50 highly variable genes from morphology at Pearson 0.4 is a benchmark result about tissue texture, not a diagnostic assay, and certainly not a substitute for sequencing a patient's tumour.
targets.statement: HEST-1k (Guillaume Jaume, Paul Doucet, Andrew Song and colleagues at Mahmood Lab, NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight) pairs spatial-transcriptomics spots with the matching histology patches and defines HEST-Benchmark: predict the expression of 50 highly variable genes from a 112 x 112 micron patch at 0.5 micron per pixel, in nine tasks covering eight cancer types, scored by Pearson correlation with leave-one-patient-out style public splits. The public result table in the repository README (re-read live on 2026-10-15, table dated 03.04.26) lists 25 publicly available models scored identically with ridge regression on PCA-reduced (256 factors) patch embeddings. The live bests are: average across tasks 0.4229 (H-Optimus-1), with GenBio-PathFM 0.4197 and H-Optimus-0 0.4150; per task, IDC 0.6024 (H-Optimus-1), PRAD 0.3913 (GenBio-PathFM), PAAD 0.5159 (Virchow), SKCM 0.6715 (GenBio-PathFM), COAD 0.3284 (GenBio-PathFM), READ 0.2421 (H-Optimus-1), CCRCC 0.2719 (Virchow2), LUNG 0.5787 (GenBio-PathFM), LYMPH_IDC 0.2842 (GenBio-PathFM); a plain ImageNet ResNet50 reaches 0.3252 on average. Three tasks sit below 0.29 and the gap between a generic ResNet and billion-parameter pathology foundation models is only about 0.10 Pearson, which says the regression head and the spatial statistics - not the encoder - may be where the remaining signal is. The benchmark data are ungated on Hugging Face (MahmoodLab/hest-bench, 42 GB in total but per-task: SKCM 0.49 GB, LUNG 0.82 GB, PAAD 1.2 GB, COAD 2.47 GB), so a single-task attack is laptop-scale, and precomputed CTransPath embeddings ship in the fm_v1 folder.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one named HEST-Benchmark task, a saved per-spot prediction matrix for the 50 benchmark genes on every test split defined by that task's splits/test_*.csv files in https://huggingface.co/datasets/MahmoodLab/hest-bench, produced by a method trained only on the corresponding train_*.csv patients, and a mean Pearson correlation computed exactly as the HEST-Library's benchmark code computes it (same gene list, same per-gene then per-split averaging), that is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum value in that task's column over ALL model rows of the live HEST-Benchmark table at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mahmoodlab/HEST/main/README.md - re-fetched and re-parsed immediately before claiming - by at least 0.015 absolute, with the gain surviving 5 random seeds reported as mean +/- std and exceeding 2x that std. The attacker must also re-run, in the same environment and splits, at least two published rows (one foundation model with precomputed or recomputable embeddings and the ResNet50 row) and land within 0.01 Pearson of their published values, or the comparison is void. No test-patient patch, expression value or summary statistic may enter training, gene filtering, normalisation, PCA fitting, hyperparameter choice or early stopping. Deliverables: pinned HEST-Library commit, dataset file sha256s, split files used, training and inference scripts, per-split prediction files, and the verbatim benchmark output for all tasks claimed.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the chosen task's folder from the ungated Hugging Face dataset (0.5-3 GB for most tasks), compares sha256s against the attacker's manifest, confirms the train/test patient lists match the published split csv files exactly, loads the attacker's predictions and recomputes the Pearson correlations with the HEST-Library's own benchmark function at a pinned commit (minutes), then re-runs the attacker's training for at least two seeds (laptop-hours) and the two baseline rows. The live record is read by curling the README and parsing the markdown table. Leakage audit: confirm that PCA, scalers, gene selection and any image-level statistics were fitted on training patients only, and that no spot from a test patient appears in training.

angles: Conventional: pan-allele modelling done with modern but small architectures trained from scratch on BD2009 - allele pseudo-sequence plus peptide, with length handling by explicit insertion/deletion encodings rather than separate models per length.

Conventional: measurement-noise-aware loss. Affinities come from different assays with different dynamic ranges; a censored-regression likelihood that respects qualitative and quantitative measurements separately is rarely used and directly addresses what limits small-allele datasets.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / soft-decision decoding): combine per-position scoring matrices for related alleles as unequal-reliability channel observations and decode with a log-likelihood-ratio rule, which is the principled version of 'borrow strength across similar HLA molecules'.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / Potts models): fit pairwise couplings between peptide positions with pseudo-likelihood direct-coupling analysis, capturing the position-position dependence that position-weight-matrix methods such as SMM-PMBEC assume away, at negligible CPU cost.

Cross-domain import (psychometrics / item response theory): alleles are items with their own difficulty and discrimination and peptides are subjects; IRT-style parameterisation handles the extreme imbalance between well-measured and barely-measured alleles better than per-allele fitting.

Cross-domain import (survey statistics / selection models): IEDB measurements are not a random sample of peptide space - they were chosen by experimenters, often guided by earlier predictors. Model that selection explicitly and reweight, which is exactly the mechanism the published study blames for the optimism gap.

Uncertainty-first: produce calibrated per-dataset confidence and report AUC together with an abstention curve; for neoantigen triage, knowing which alleles the model cannot handle is worth as much as the mean AUC.
targets.name: Peptide-MHC class I binding: beat NetMHCpan's blind-set AUC on the frozen public IEDB BD2009-to-Blind benchmark

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best reference blind AUC by >= 0.02 on the 20 smallest Blind datasets (those the published analysis identifies as least reliable, where size and diversity drive the cross-validation-to-blind gap), under the same training restriction, showing that small-allele transfer is improvable.

Shrink the published cross-validation-to-blind optimism gap: report, for the attacker's method, the gap between cross-validated and blind mean AUC and show it is smaller than NetMHCpan's published gap (0.9147 versus 0.8830, i.e. 0.0317) by at least 0.01 while blind AUC is not worse than the reference. A calibration result about honest evaluation, independently checkable.

A leakage-quantification result of record: measure how much apparent blind AUC a modern pretrained predictor gains on this benchmark purely because its training data include the Blind measurements, by comparing it against the same architecture trained only on BD2009. Reported as a methodological finding, not as a record.

pitfalls: Training-data contamination is the defining trap: every modern peptide-MHC predictor was trained on data that include the Blind measurements, so running one of them on this benchmark produces a meaningless number. The claim must document the provenance of every component, including language-model weights.

Near-duplicate peptides between BD2009 and Blind for the same allele: the published analysis shows similarity is not the main driver of the optimism gap, but a claimed win must still report the similarity distribution and show the gain is not confined to near-duplicates.

Dataset-set drift: the published tables cover 87 (allele, length) datasets with both cross-validation and blind values while the Blind set as a whole contains 90; averaging over a different dataset set, or weighting by dataset size instead of averaging per dataset, moves the mean by more than the 0.01 bar.

Threshold and metric conventions: binder/non-binder thresholds (500 nM) and the handling of qualitative measurements change AUC; only the benchmark's own convention counts, and the skeptic must recompute rather than trust reported numbers.
