pitfalls: Approximate decompositions (fidelity < 1) and stabilizer extent are different quantities; only exact equality counts.
Orbit confusion: |T>, |H> and the face state |F> are named inconsistently across papers; fix the state vector explicitly and compare only to bounds for the same Clifford orbit.
Coefficients recognised numerically must be verified exactly; PSLQ can return wrong algebraic numbers at low precision.
This area moves monthly (2605.28586, 2610.06819, 2610.17500 all in 2026); re-search arXiv immediately before claiming.
targets.statement: The stabilizer rank chi(psi) is the fewest stabilizer states whose linear combination equals psi exactly; for m copies of a magic state it controls the runtime of stabilizer-rank simulators of Clifford+T circuits (Bravyi and Gosset 2016; Bravyi, Browne, Calpin, Campbell, Gosset, Howard 2019). Any exact decomposition of psi^{(x)m} into r stabilizer states gives an exponent alpha <= log2(r)/m. For the H-type state |T> = (|0> + e^{i pi/4}|1>)/sqrt2, Hammam Qassim, Hakop Pashayan and David Gosset (arXiv:2106.07740) proved alpha <= 0.3963; Farrokh Labib and Vincent Russo (arXiv:2605.28586, May 2026) gave new qutrit-orbit bounds and a closed-form four-copy decomposition matching log2(3)/4 ~ 0.3962 for what they call the qubit T-type orbit (state names differ between papers). For the face-centre magic state, Samuel Bevins (arXiv:2610.17500, 12 Oct 2026) built a 24-term decomposition of 12 copies from two 15-term identities and proved alpha_F <= 3/8. Small-m exact ranks remain open beyond a few copies, and the area is moving monthly.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for psi in {|T> (H-type, the state above), the face-centre state |F> as defined in arXiv:2610.17500}, an explicit list of r stabilizer states on m qubits (each as a stabilizer tableau plus phase, or a quadratic-form/affine-space description) and exact coefficients in an explicit number field (Q(zeta_8) suffices for |T>) whose sum equals psi^{(x)m} EXACTLY, with log2(r)/m STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the best published exponent for that orbit found by an arXiv search re-run immediately before claiming (0.3963 for |T> per arXiv:2106.07740 and 3/8 for |F> per arXiv:2610.17500 on 2026-10-15), by at least 0.001; OR, without beating the exponent, r STRICTLY LESS than the smallest published exact decomposition for that specific m (m <= 12), with the published value cited.
targets.verification_method: Expand each stabilizer state to its 2^m amplitude vector exactly (sympy over the cyclotomic field, or integer vectors over Z[zeta_8] scaled by powers of sqrt2), sum with the coefficients, and compare entrywise to the exact tensor power; m <= 16 takes seconds. Independently confirm each listed state is a stabilizer state (tableau generators commute and are independent, or the affine/quadratic form check). Recompute log2(r)/m and compare with the live papers.

angles: Universal-potential embeddings as features: frozen MACE-MP / CHGNet / ORB node embeddings pooled per structure feeding gradient boosting or a small MLP; cheap on CPU and strong on elastic and phonon targets (check that pretraining data do not contain the targets).

Physics-informed phonon target: the last phonon DOS peak correlates with the highest optical frequency; predict it from a universal potential's Gamma-point Hessian (a few seconds per structure) and learn only the residual.
Elasticity priors: compute bulk and shear moduli with a universal potential via strain-stress fits, then delta-learn log_kvrh and log_gvrh from those estimates.
Dielectric: use Clausius-Mossotti style polarizability sums over ions plus band-gap proxies as features; refractive index scales with gap.
Statistics: multi-seed ensembles and hyperparameter search inside the inner folds only; report paired fold-wise comparisons with the leaderboard entry.
targets.name: Matbench v0.1 medium tasks (phonons, dielectric, expt_is_metal, log_gvrh, log_kvrh, perovskites): beat the verified leaderboard score with CPU-trained models

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best leaderboard entry that uses no structure (composition-only) on a 'structure required' task by at least 10% relative, with the same protocol.
A single CPU-trained model architecture that ranks first or second on at least three of the six tasks simultaneously under the protocol.

pitfalls: Fold leakage: hyperparameters tuned on outer test folds, or features from a model pretrained on Materials Project data containing the same structures' target labels (elastic moduli, dielectric constants), invalidate the claim.

Universal potentials pretrained on MPtrj saw the structures but not phonon/dielectric/elastic labels; that is allowed only if stated, but any model trained on MP elasticity or dielectric labels is leakage.

Unverified literature numbers: many papers quote Matbench scores without the official protocol or with different folds; only protocol-compliant fold predictions count, and the leaderboard's 'verified' value is the bar.
Do not compare log10(GPa) MAE with GPa MAE, or ROC-AUC with accuracy.
targets.statement: Matbench v0.1 (Alexander Dunn, Qi Wang, Alex Ganose, Daniel Dopp and Anubhav Jain, npj Comput. Mater. 6, 138, 2020) scores materials-property models by nested 5-fold cross-validation with fixed folds; its verified leaderboard (checked live 2026-10-15) lists: matbench_phonons (1,265 structures, last phonon DOS peak) 28.7606 cm^-1 by MegNet (kgcnn v2.1.0); matbench_dielectric (4,764) 0.2711 by MODNet v0.1.12; matbench_expt_is_metal (4,921, ROC-AUC) 0.9209 by AMMExpress v2020; matbench_log_gvrh and matbench_log_kvrh (10,987) 0.0670 and 0.0491 log10(GPa) by coNGN; matbench_perovskites (18,928) 0.0269 eV/unit cell by coGN. These sizes are trainable on a laptop CPU in hours to days. The four smallest-data tasks (steels, expt_gap, glass, jdft2d) are covered by a separate entry and excluded here.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a complete Matbench v0.1 record for one of the six named tasks (predictions for all 5 test folds produced with the official matbench package folds, models trained only on each fold's training data) whose mean score is STRICTLY BETTER (direction: min for MAE, max for ROC-AUC) than the verified leaderboard value for that task on https://matbench.materialsproject.org/ re-fetched immediately before claiming, by at least the larger of 2% relative and the fold-to-fold standard deviation of the best listed entry divided by sqrt(5); AND re-running the saved per-fold models reproduces the predictions; AND a literature search finds no published Matbench-protocol score for that task that is better than the claim (reported with the claim either way).
targets.verification_method: Checker (< 1 hour for prediction checks): load the claim's matbench results json (the format produced by MatbenchBenchmark.to_file); confirm task name, fold indices and that fold test indices match the official KFold (random_state 18012019, shuffle); recompute fold scores from predictions and the matbench dataset labels; re-run inference for one random fold from the saved model; compare with the live leaderboard value.

angles: Baxter's own 1968 route was a variational CTM-like approximation; rerun a modern CTM (Nishino-Okunishi CTMRG) on the monomer-dimer vertex model in arbitrary precision.
From quantum many-body physics: the monomer-dimer transfer matrix maps to a hard-core boson chain; a VUMPS fixed point in high precision is an independent second method.
From combinatorics: Kong's fixed-density maximisation and the Friedland-Peled pressure inequalities give two-sided checks; use them as a sanity frame around the high-precision estimate.
Exact strip free energies f_L via sparse power iteration on 2^L-state transfer matrices (L <= 26 fits in RAM) plus exponential-correction fits.
targets.name: Monomer-dimer constant of the square lattice: more than the 11-12 decimals published by Kong (2006)

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous enclosure of h2 certifying at least 12 decimals (improving Friedland-Peled's 8 certified decimals and making Kong's bracket rigorous or not), via Friedland-Peled transfer-matrix inequalities evaluated in exact or interval arithmetic with published certificate vectors.

At least 15 decimals, by two independent methods, of the square-lattice monomer-dimer free energy at another standard monomer activity reported in the literature with fewer digits (for example Kong's fixed-density values f2(1/2) = 0.633195588930), stating the published comparator with its source.

pitfalls: Normalisation traps: per site vs per dimer, natural log vs e^h2 (1.9402...), and the pure-dimer constant (Catalan/pi = 0.2915...) are all different numbers that circulate under the same name.
Kong's '0.662798972834' is quoted with 12 decimals but he states 11 correct digits; the comparator is the bracket, not the last printed digit.
Agreement of successive truncations of one method is not two methods; the criterion needs genuinely different algorithms.
Float64 limits agreement to about 15 digits; a 20-digit claim needs multiprecision linear algebra end to end.
targets.statement: The monomer-dimer entropy h2 of the square lattice (log of the number of matchings per site of the n x n grid as n grows; Hosoya index growth, OEIS A028420 counts the finite boards) has no closed form. Baxter's 1968 heuristic gave e^h2 = 1.940215351; Shmuel Friedland and Uri Peled (Adv. Appl. Math. 2005, arXiv math/0402009) certified 8 decimals; Yong Kong (Phys. Rev. E 74 (2006) 061102, arXiv cond-mat/0610690) maximised fixed-density entropies to get h2 = 0.662798972834 with bracket 0.662798972831 < h2 < 0.662798972845 ('11 correct digits'); Paolo Butera, Paul Federbush and Marco Pernici (arXiv 1305.7028, 2013) give 0.662798972(1) from series. No OEIS entry holds the digits of h2 (search checked 2026-10-15) and Steven Finch's 2020-2024 errata quote only 0.66279897.... At unit monomer activity the model has no phase transition (Heilmann-Lieb) and correlations decay exponentially, so high-precision CTM or boundary-MPS methods should give many more digits on a laptop.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a decimal value of h2 (natural log, per site) with at least 20 decimals such that (a) two independent methods agree on all claimed decimals (for example CTM or VUMPS on the monomer-dimer transfer operator, and exact strip transfer matrices of width up to about 24 with extrapolation), (b) the value lies inside Kong's bracket [0.662798972831, 0.662798972845] and agrees with 0.662798972834 to its 12 decimals up to final-digit rounding, (c) the digits are stable over at least three truncation increases, and (d) an arXiv/Google Scholar/OEIS search, re-run immediately before claiming, finds no published value with as many decimals. Direction: more digits.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic (< 1 hour): rerun both programs at the two largest truncations in multiprecision; check digit agreement, check the value against Kong's bracket, and reproduce OEIS A028420 terms n <= 14 with the strip transfer code as a correctness test of the state space.

angles: Flip-graph search (the method behind recent matrix-multiplication rank records) is already in polytof; push it on the biggest tensors (Mod Adder_1024, Ham15 high, Grover_5, Adder_8) with long runs and plateau moves, since the paper's runs were budgeted in CPU-minutes.
Basis change first: the CP rank is invariant under GL(n,F_2) but search difficulty depends on nnz; anneal over CNOT basis changes to minimise nnz or tensor slice ranks before decomposition.

Import from coding theory: T-count reduction is Reed-Muller decoding (punctured RM(n-4, n)*); use list decoders and information-set decoding from classical decoding literature on the signature, as in TODD's lineage.

Import from algebraic complexity: GF(2^k) multiplication tensors are bilinear maps whose rank has been studied via Chudnovsky-type interpolation on curves; use those constructions to seed 05xx/07xx searches.
Import from SAT: for small tensors (n <= 20) encode 'rank <= r' as SAT with symmetry breaking and either find a lower decomposition or produce a DRAT proof (partial win p2).
targets.name: Toffoli-count and T-count records: fewer non-Clifford gates for a benchmark circuit tensor than the Khoruzhii-Gelss-Pokutta (polytof) table

partial_wins.statement: A strictly lower Toffoli (CP) count than the live table for some GF(2^k) multiplication tensor (07xx/05xx, k = 2..10) or AES S-box circuit tensor, with the same exact check; note that for the base 05xx tensors this equals a new upper bound on the bilinear complexity of GF(2^k) multiplication, which must also be checked against the classical literature on that problem.

A certified optimality proof for a table row whose optimality is not already published: an exhaustive or SAT/DRAT certificate that no decomposition with (table value - 1) terms exists for that tensor variant, re-checkable in under an hour.
An independent re-verification audit of all decompositions in data/paper/ that reports any table value not reproduced by its posted decomposition.

pitfalls: Toffoli count (CP rank) and T-count (Waring rank) are different columns; beating one does not beat the other, and gadget-based counts (ATQ 'gadgets' files) are a different accounting.

Tensor variants differ: 01xx (from AlphaTensor-Quantum) and 08xx (compiled from Vandaele's circuits) can have different n and nnz for the 'same' circuit, and 05xx/03xx/07xx are different representations of GF(2^k) multiplication. Compare only within the same tensor ID.

CP equality is required only modulo quadratic and linear terms; a checker that demands exact equality of all entries will wrongly reject valid schemes, and one that ignores the cubic diagonal-pattern conventions will wrongly accept invalid ones. Use the repository's verification as a second opinion.
Some rows may already be optimal: Mazumder (arXiv:2610.01024, Oct 2026) gives an isotropy lower bound certifying many phase-polynomial blocks T-optimal; check it before spending compute.
The table moves (last commit 2026-10-12); a value beaten in a stale clone may already be updated upstream.
targets.statement: For a quantum circuit over {CNOT, Toffoli/CCZ, H}, the non-Clifford part can be gathered into one diagonal phase operator given by a cubic phase polynomial over F_2, stored as a symmetric 3-tensor. Its CP rank (up to quadratic and linear terms) is the Toffoli/CCZ count and its Waring rank is the T-count (Amy and Mosca; Heyfron and Campbell). AlphaTensor-Quantum (Ruiz, Laakkonen, Bausch, ..., van de Wetering, Fawzi, Meichanetzidis, Kohli; Nature Machine Intelligence 2025) set T-count records on a standard suite of arithmetic benchmarks with large TPU budgets. Kirill Khoruzhii, Patrick Gelss and Sebastian Pokutta (arXiv:2602.15285, Feb 2026) then matched or beat every reported Toffoli and T-count with CPU-minute algebraic methods (basis-change optimisation, symplectic Gaussian elimination, flip-graph search, FastTODD) and keep a public table of best known CP rank and Waring rank per tensor in their repository (docs/tensors.md, last commit 2026-10-12). Examples on 2026-10-15: Barenco Tof_10 (n=50) CP 16 / T-count 83; Mod Adder_1024 (n=332) CP 128 / T 573; Ham15 (high) (n=351) CP 155 / T 643; QCLA Mod_7 (n=84) CP 37 / T 153; GF(2^10) multiplication CP 33 / T 173; Hamming-weight n=20 CP 18 / T 109; Unary iteration n=5 CP 31 / T 127. The tensors (.npy) and the decompositions behind each number ship with the repository, so a lower count is an exactly checkable object. Large tensors (n > 60) and the newest families (AES S-box circuits added 2026-10-12) have seen the least search.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for some tensor ID listed in the live polytof table (https://github.com/ZIB-IOL/polytof/blob/main/docs/tensors.md, re-fetched live immediately before claiming), an explicit decomposition with STRICTLY FEWER terms (direction: min, margin >= 1 term) than the listed CP value (Toffoli count) or the listed Waring value (T-count) for that tensor ID, such that: (a) for CP, the list of r triples of binary vectors (u_t, v_t, w_t) reproduces the tensor's cubic monomials x_i x_j x_k (i<j<k) exactly over F_2 after symmetrisation, with only quadratic and linear differences allowed, as checked by an independent script AND by polytof's scripts/verify_paper_schemes.py; for Waring, the r binary vectors a_t reproduce the full signature (phase polynomial) of that tensor variant exactly in the convention polytof and AlphaTensor-Quantum use; (b) the same tensor variant (01xx vs 08xx vs 07xx) is used as the table row; (c) for at least one claimed circuit the decomposition is turned back into a CNOT + Toffoli/T circuit and checked exactly equal (up to global phase) to the original benchmark circuit by a path-sum or statevector equivalence check; and (d) an arXiv search finds no lower published count for that circuit (including Mazumder arXiv:2610.01024 lower bounds, which may prove the table value optimal).
targets.verification_method: Clone https://github.com/ZIB-IOL/polytof (tensors in data/tensors/*.npy: row 0 = dims, rows 1.. = nonzero (i,j,k) with i<j<k). Independent checker in numpy uint8: build the cubic monomial set of the target; for a CP claim expand sum_t sym(u_t (x) v_t (x) w_t) mod 2 and compare the i<j<k part exactly; for a Waring claim compute sum_t a_t (x) a_t (x) a_t mod 2 over all index patterns used by the repository's own Waring check and compare. Run scripts/verify_paper_schemes.py style verification on the new scheme. For circuit-level confirmation (n <= ~30 qubits), synthesise the phase operator from the decomposition, conjugate by the recorded Clifford/basis-change, and compare to the original .qc/.qasm with a path-sum checker (e.g. Feynman's feynver) or exact statevector on random basis inputs plus a symbolic check. Re-fetch tensors.md and compare the count.

angles: Colour-permutation compression: count colourings up to the action of S_q on colours (set partitions of the boundary) so the state space for q = 4 grows like Bell-type numbers, not q^width; Lundow and Markstrom used this only up to modest widths on 2006 hardware.

From quantum many-body physics: for the non-critical square-lattice cases, VUMPS/CTMRG in high precision gives the p1 digits quickly and suggests which boundary type converges fastest for rigorous use.
For the cubic lattice, increase the cross-section (6x6, 6x8 tori) with the same compression and a matrix-free power iteration; the 3-colouring bracket is still about 1e-3 wide.

From representation theory: block-diagonalise by translation momentum and reflection symmetry of the cross-section; the leading eigenvector lives in the trivial sector, which shrinks the problem further.
targets.name: Ground-state entropy of Potts antiferromagnets (proper colourings): tighten the certified bounds of Lundow and Markstrom (2008) for 4- and 5-colourings of the square grid or 3- and 4-colourings of the cubic lattice

partial_wins.statement: At least 15 decimals of W_sq(4) (or W_sq(5)) by two independent non-rigorous methods (corner transfer matrix or VUMPS, and strip transfer matrices with extrapolation), lying inside the Lundow-Markstrom bracket and agreeing with the series value 2.336056641 within 1e-9.
An independent reproduction of Lundow and Markstrom's eigenvalue table for 4-colourings of the square grid up to their largest width, with exact or multiprecision eigenvalues released as data.

pitfalls: The widely quoted Monte Carlo value 2.3370(7) for W_sq(4) is far less precise than (and sits above) the rigorous bracket; using it as the bar produces false 'improvements'.
Vertex colourings vs edge colourings: the Kondev-Henley four-colouring model is an edge-colouring model with a different entropy.
Open, cylinder and torus transfer matrices bound W in specific directions only for the right parities and boundary choices; check the inequality's hypotheses for each matrix.
Per-site vs per-row normalisation and natural log vs W: report W per site as in Lundow-Markstrom.
targets.statement: The zero-temperature entropy of the q-state Potts antiferromagnet is the growth rate W per site of proper q-colourings. Lieb solved q = 3 on the square lattice ((4/3)^(3/2)); q = 4 and 5 on the square lattice and q = 3, 4 on the cubic lattice have no closed form. Per Hakan Lundow and Klas Markstrom (LMS J. Comput. Math. (2008), 'Exact and approximate compression of transfer matrices for graph homomorphisms', open access) give the best rigorous bounds known to us: 2.336056640723116 <= W_sq(4) <= 2.33606820555777; 3.2504049231640764 <= W_sq(5) <= 3.250407145038276; 1.4460096817417 <= W_c(3) <= 1.4470681274660; 2.0343787307189 <= W_c(4) <= 2.0652128520667. A large-q series quoted there gives W_sq(4) = 2.336056641 +- 1e-9 (heuristic). The Monte Carlo value W_sq(4) = 2.3370(7) of Robert Shrock and Shan-Ho Tsai (1997), still cited in later papers, sits about 1.4 standard errors above the rigorous bracket and is roughly 1e5 times less precise. Since q = 4, 5 on the square lattice are non-critical, both tighter rigorous bounds (larger transfer matrices with symmetry compression; their cubic bounds used only 4x4 to 6x6 cross-sections) and many more non-rigorous digits are laptop-reachable. No later improvement was found (search 2026-10-15).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous bound strictly improving one of the eight published bounds above (upper smaller or lower larger), by at least 1e-9 for W_sq(4) or W_sq(5) and at least 1e-6 for W_c(3) or W_c(4), with the transfer-matrix definition and a nonnegative test vector whose Collatz-Wielandt ratios (or the exact eigenvalue inequality used by Lundow and Markstrom, cited by equation) a skeptic recomputes in exact or outward-rounded arithmetic, AND an arXiv/Google Scholar search re-run immediately before claiming that finds no published bound at least as good.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic (< 1 hour per certificate at moderate width): rebuild the colour-compressed transfer matrix for the stated width and boundary type, check the claimed vector is nonnegative, compute the ratios exactly or with interval arithmetic, and apply the stated inequality; reproduce two smaller published widths first.

angles: Extend Couronne's automaton to loop length 28 with a compact state encoding and disk-backed sparse iteration; the bound sequence was still dropping about 1.9e-3 per two units of loop length.
From formal languages: walks avoiding a finite set of short loops form a regular language; minimise the DFA (Hopcroft) and merge equivalent states before the eigenvalue step.
From numerical linear algebra: certify with a Lanczos-improved test vector rather than plain power iteration; a better vector at the same automaton size gives a better certified ratio.
Lower bound: Jensen's bridge counts can be extended with modern transfer-matrix code and modular arithmetic; Kesten's method converts every extra length directly into a bound.
targets.name: Self-avoiding walks: a certified bound on the square-lattice connective constant beating Couronne's upper bound 2.662342426 (2022) or Jensen's lower bound 2.625622 (2004)

partial_wins.statement: A certified improvement, by at least 1e-6, of the best published rigorous bound for the triangular, kagome or 4.8^2 lattice (starting from Jensen 2004 Table 3; the claimant must show by search that no later bound beats theirs), same certificate rules.

An independent reimplementation reproducing Couronne's 2.662342426 at loop length 26 (or his shorter-loop bounds) in less than his reported one week of computation; reproduction only, but it validates the code for the main attempt.

pitfalls: Estimates of mu (2.6381585303...) are not bounds; an 'upper bound' below 2.6381585 indicates a bug, not a record.
Counting walks with finite memory overcounts only if the forbidden-loop set is applied consistently from both ends; an inconsistent automaton gives a too-small, invalid 'upper bound'.
For hexagonal and 3.12^2 lattices the connective constant is known exactly (Duminil-Copin-Smirnov; A249776); bounds there are not open problems.
Floating-point spectral radii are not certificates; outward rounding or exact arithmetic is required.
targets.statement: The square-lattice connective constant is estimated as mu = 2.63815853032790(3) (Jesper Jacobsen, Christian Scullard and Anthony Guttmann 2016; OEIS A387897, Wikipedia 'Connective constant'), but rigorous bounds are much looser. Upper: Olivier Couronne (arXiv 2211.16146, 2022) modified the finite-memory automaton of Andre Ponitz and Peter Tittmann (2000, 2.679193) and, with loops up to length 26 (one week, 32 GB), proved mu < 2.662342426. Lower: Iwan Jensen (arXiv cond-mat/0409381, J. Phys. A 2004) used Kesten's irreducible-bridge method to get mu > 2.625622. Jensen's Table 3 also lists rigorous brackets for the triangular (4.118935, 4.25152 by Sven Erick Alm), kagome (2.548497, 2.590301) and 4.8^2 (1.804596, 1.82926) lattices. Qidong He (J. Phys. A 58 (2025) 505003, arXiv 2508.01993) published open software (github.com/qidong-he/weighted_connective_constant) for Alm-type upper bounds on these lattices. Couronne's sequence of bounds (2.669575, 2.666665, 2.664196, 2.662342 for growing loop length) is still improving at the last step.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous bound on the square-lattice connective constant strictly better than the best published bound found by an arXiv/Google Scholar search re-run immediately before claiming (currently upper 2.662342426, lower 2.625622), by at least 1e-6, with a checkable certificate: for upper bounds, the automaton/transfer matrix definition plus a nonnegative test vector whose Collatz-Wielandt ratio is verified in exact or outward-rounded arithmetic; for lower bounds, the exact integer bridge counts used, with a program that recomputes the bound from them, and the counts reproducing Jensen's published values at all lengths he lists.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic: for an upper bound, rebuild the automaton from the stated loop list for a small loop length and match Couronne's or Ponitz-Tittmann's published value, then check the claimed certificate vector's ratios with exact arithmetic (minutes to hours depending on state count; the certificate can be checked by streaming). For a lower bound, recompute the bound from the supplied bridge counts and spot-check counts at small lengths by brute force.

angles: Port SAWdoubler (written for sc, bcc, fcc) to Z^4: the length-doubling identity c_{2n} = sum over pairs of n-step walks with inclusion-exclusion over shared sites only needs the lattice neighbour structure and its symmetry group; exploit the 384-element hyperoctahedral group to store walks up to symmetry.
Import from database engineering: the inclusion-exclusion step is a giant subset-join; external-memory sort-merge on a 1 TB disk replaces the cluster memory Schram et al. used.
Import from coding theory: hash the site sets of half-walks into Bloom-filter-like signatures to prune non-intersecting pairs before exact checks.
Do odd n by c_{2n+1} via an asymmetric split (n, n+1); computing n = 25 first is cheaper and already a record.
Cross-check against the lace-expansion route: Clisby-Liang-Slade show that polygon counts plus lace graphs give c_n; a second method for the same term is exactly what the two-run rule needs.
targets.name: Self-avoiding walks: an exact count c_n beyond the published record on the 4D/5D hypercubic, bcc, fcc or simple cubic lattice

partial_wins.statement: New exact terms for a related series on Z^4 or Z^5 beyond the published record: self-avoiding polygon counts p_n, or the sum of squared end-to-end distances, with the same two-run agreement rule.

A clean, documented port of SAWdoubler (or an independent length-doubling implementation) to Z^d, d = 4..6, that reproduces all published c_n up to n = 24 for each d; reproduction only, but checkable and a prerequisite for the main win.

pitfalls: OEIS 'data' fields are truncated; the b-files and the Clisby-Liang-Slade data page hold the full records. Check both.
Lattice naming: OEIS 'hexagonal' sometimes means triangular; A001666 is 'b.c.c. version 2'. Use the exact definitions of the record papers.
Off-by-one and symmetry-factor errors give plausible-looking but wrong integers; reproduction of all lower terms plus a second independent run is mandatory.
Integer overflow above 2^64 (c_25 in 5D is about 5.6e23); use 128-bit or arbitrary precision accumulators.

A 2025 Utrecht bachelor thesis (Marloes de Groot, 'Enumerating self-avoiding walks by k-splitting', studenttheses.uu.nl handle 20.500.12932/48786) extends length doubling; its abstract reports no new counts, but read the full PDF before claiming novelty for any lattice.
targets.statement: The number c_n of n-step self-avoiding walks is known exactly to n = 79 on the square lattice (Iwan Jensen), 36 on the simple cubic lattice (Raoul Schram, Gerard Barkema, Rob Bisseling 2011), 28 on bcc and 24 on fcc (Schram, Barkema, Bisseling, Nathan Clisby 2017), and 24 on the hypercubic lattices Z^d for every d >= 4 (Clisby, Richard Liang, Gordon Slade 2007, lace expansion; polygons to 26 in d = 4, 24 in d = 5, 6). The d >= 4 series have not been extended since 2007 (checked 2026-10-15), and the length-doubling program SAWdoubler (public, v2.0.1 2017, shipped with sc/bcc/fcc lattice files only) has not been reported on Z^4 or Z^5. Length doubling costs about O(2^N Z_N) for half-length N (Schram et al. 2011); the sc n = 36 record took 50,000 CPU-hours (N = 18, Z_18 = 2.24e12, 48 symmetries), while Z^4 n = 26 has N = 13, Z_13 = 8.75e10 and 384 symmetries, well under a thousandth of the work. The limit is memory for the subset counters, so this is a laptop-days, disk-assisted computation.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an exact integer c_n for one lattice in {Z^4, Z^5, Z^6, sc, bcc, fcc} with n strictly greater than the largest n in BOTH the lattice's OEIS b-file (re-fetched immediately before claiming) and the Clisby-Liang-Slade data page / Schram et al. papers, AND no arXiv/Google Scholar search finds a published value for that (lattice, n); AND the value is computed by two independent runs that agree exactly (different split points n = a + b of length doubling, or length doubling vs. a lace-expansion or transfer-style method), AND the same code reproduces every published c_m for m <= the previous record on that lattice.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic (< 1 h): re-run the claimant's code to reproduce all published terms up to the old record on that lattice (minutes to an hour), check exact agreement of the two independent runs' outputs for the new term, and sanity-check the new term against ratio analysis (c_n / c_{n-2} consistent with the known growth constant mu, e.g. mu ~ 6.774 for Z^4) and parity/symmetry divisibility (c_n divisible by 2d). Full re-computation of the new term is laptop-hours and can be done after the panel.

angles: Ghost-first route: use Zauner.jl to compute the ghost fiducial for a chosen d >= 194 at high precision, then Galois-conjugate (sign switch of sqrt(Delta_0)) by recognising overlaps as algebraic numbers, and Newton-refine; a successful run is a data point for the Appleby-Flammia-Kopp conjectures beyond d = 100.

Independent numerical route: impose Zauner (order-3) or Scott's F_a/F_b symmetry and minimise sum_p |<psi|D_p psi>|^4 with FFT-based O(d^2 log d) evaluations and many L-BFGS restarts; seed with Stark-unit or ghost phases to cut restarts.

Import from signal processing: SIC fiducials are flat-ambiguity Gabor windows; Gerchberg-Saxton-style alternating projections between fiducial and ambiguity-function constraints are a fast alternative to gradient descent.

Dimension choice: favour d with many small factors (e.g. 196, 198, 200, 210) where extra Clifford symmetries reduce the search, or d whose admissible tuple has a short word length l in the Zauner.jl tables (cheaper ghost evaluation).
targets.name: SIC-POVMs: the first publicly posted numerical Weyl-Heisenberg SIC fiducial in a dimension d >= 194 (outside known families)

partial_wins.statement: The first PUBLICLY posted numerical fiducial (60-digit refined, same tolerance) for some d in 152..193 not in any posted list; Grassl reports solutions exist there, so this is a public-data contribution only.

A numerical SIC for some d >= 101 found by an independent method (not Zauner.jl) whose overlap phases match (or provably fail to match) the Appleby-Flammia-Kopp ghost prediction for that d: either outcome is an independent test of the 2025 conjectures. A mismatch must be confirmed by two independent computations.

A new Clifford-orbit class of SIC in some d <= 90 missing from both Scott's putative complete list and the Appleby-Flammia-Kopp admissible-tuple tables (shown inequivalent under the extended Clifford group via overlap-phase multisets); this would contradict two completeness conjectures and needs exceptional scrutiny.

pitfalls: Near-misses: L-BFGS converges to vectors with deviation ~1e-6 that are not SICs; only the 60-digit Newton refinement to < 1e-40 counts.

Known dimensions are scattered across sources: Scott 2017 (195, 199, 228, 259, 323), Fibonacci-Lucas (844, and 1299 per Grassl's 2021 talk), the Stark-unit tables (e.g. 199, 292, 487, 628, 787, ... 39604) and the d = 100 examples of arXiv:2501.03970; check all of them.
A Zauner.jl-generated SIC is the output of a public recipe; it must be labelled as such and is not independent confirmation of the Appleby-Flammia-Kopp conjectures.
A numerical fiducial, however precise, is not a proof of existence (the SIC equations are overdetermined, so interval Newton does not apply directly); say 'numerical'.
Convention mismatches (phase factor tau = -e^{i pi/d}, index ordering) change individual overlaps but not their moduli; the checker uses moduli.
targets.statement: A SIC-POVM in dimension d is d^2 unit vectors in C^d with |<psi_j|psi_k>|^2 = 1/(d+1) for j != k; Zauner's conjecture says they exist for every d, as Weyl-Heisenberg orbits of a fiducial vector. Numerical fiducials: Andrew Scott and Markus Grassl (JMP 2010) for all d <= 67; Scott (arXiv:1703.03993) a putatively complete list of known-symmetry solutions for d <= 90, one Zauner-symmetric solution for every d <= 121, and higher-symmetry solutions for d = 124, 143, 147, 168, 172, 195, 199, 228, 259, 323; Grassl reports numerical solutions for all d <= 193 (CodEx talk abstract, 2021, which also mentions exact solutions in d = 844 and 1299). Families beyond that: Fibonacci-Lucas dimensions (Grassl-Scott 2017: 4, 8, 19, 48, 124, 323, 844, ...), Stark-unit constructions for prime d = n^2+3 (Appleby, Bengtsson, Grassl, Harrison, McConnell 2022; up to d = 19603) and for d = n^2+3 = 4p (Bengtsson, Grassl, McConnell, arXiv:2403.02872; up to d = 39604), all tabulated on Grassl's SIC page (last updated 2022-11-08). Crucially, Marcus Appleby, Steven Flammia and Gene Kopp (arXiv:2501.03970, Jan 2025) give an explicit conditional construction of a putatively complete set of Weyl-Heisenberg SICs in EVERY dimension d > 3 (ghost SICs from Shintani-Faddeev modular cocycle values, Galois-conjugate to SICs assuming the order-1 abelian Stark conjecture and a special-value identity), released as the Julia package Zauner.jl, and computed four inequivalent numerical SICs in d = 100 (three new). So for d >= 194 outside the families above, no numerical fiducial appears to be publicly posted (checked 2026-10-15), but a public recipe exists; a new-dimension numerical fiducial is a data contribution and a test of the Appleby-Flammia-Kopp conjectures, not new existence mathematics.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a fiducial vector psi in C^d for some d >= 194 such that (a) after Newton refinement in mpmath at 60 digits, max_{p != 0} | |<psi|D_p psi>|^2 - 1/(d+1) | < 1e-40 over all d^2 - 1 Weyl-Heisenberg displacement operators D_p (Appleby convention), with |psi| = 1; (b) d does not appear (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) on Grassl's SIC page (http://s208785153.online.de/SICPOVM/), on Flammia's exact-SIC page, in Scott 2017's list, in the Fibonacci-Lucas and Stark-unit papers (arXiv:1707.02944, 2112.05552, 2403.02872), in Appleby-Flammia-Kopp (arXiv:2501.03970) or the Zauner.jl documentation, and an arXiv/Google Scholar search for 'SIC' with 'd = <value>' finds no published fiducial for that d; and (c) the claim states which method produced it (independent numerical search vs the Zauner.jl ghost construction), since only the former is independent evidence for the conjectures behind the latter.
targets.verification_method: Checker (< 30 min for d <= 400): load psi (complex, >= 60 digits), normalise; compute all overlaps <psi|D_{p} psi> via the FFT identity in double, then for the max-deviation check repeat in mpmath at 60 digits (d^2 overlaps x O(d) each; ~10^7 multiprecision operations at d = 200); assert deviation < 1e-40; confirm d is not in the known-dimension list compiled from the cited sources.

angles: Newman-Ziff union-find sweeps with wrapping probabilities on tori: at the threshold the wrapping probability tends to a universal value with small finite-size corrections, which gives 1e-6-1e-7 precision on a laptop for planar lattices.

From algebraic combinatorics: Jacobsen-Scullard critical polynomials P_B(p) on n x n bases of the periodic tiling give root sequences that converge fast; even small bases often beat Monte Carlo by orders of magnitude.

From computational geometry: generate each 2-uniform tiling programmatically from its vertex configuration (Grunbaum-Shephard numbering) and verify it by vertex-type counts before any percolation run.
Use the site-to-bond mapping on the covering (line) lattice as a cross-check where a two-uniform lattice's covering lattice has a known bond threshold.
targets.name: Site percolation thresholds of the 20 two-uniform lattices: beat the 4-digit values of Neher, Mecke and Wagner (2008) listed on Wikipedia's percolation-threshold tables

partial_wins.statement: All 20 two-uniform site thresholds to uncertainty at most 2e-5 each, same two-method and reproduction rules, published as a table with code.
An independent determination, to at least 7 digits, of a 'citation needed' bond threshold in the same Wikipedia table, either confirming it or showing a discrepancy larger than its stated error bar.

pitfalls: Lattice identity: two-uniform numbering varies between sources; a precise value for the wrong tiling is a false win. Match the vertex-type fractions and z-bar in the Wikipedia row.
Monte Carlo error bars that ignore finite-size corrections or seed correlations are too small; require the second method.
Critical-polynomial roots are estimates that converge from one side for some lattices and oscillate for others; the error bar must come from the observed convergence, not the last difference.
Some 'citation needed' bond values may come from unpublished critical-polynomial runs; a discrepancy with them is reportable but not by itself a record.
targets.statement: The Wikipedia 'Percolation threshold' page (section '2-uniform lattices', checked 2026-10-15) lists site thresholds for the 20 two-uniform tilings, all from Richard Neher, Klaus Mecke and Herbert Wagner (J. Stat. Mech. 2008; arXiv 0708.3250 with supplementary table arXiv 0708.3251), obtained by Newman-Ziff simulations on L = 64..1024 with about 2e-4 precision: e.g. #41 (1/2)(3,4,3,12)+(1/2)(3,12^2) 0.7680(2), #42 0.7157(2), #36 0.6808(2), #15 0.6499(2), #34 0.6329(2), #16 0.6286(2). The bond thresholds on the same rows have 8 digits (several marked 'citation needed'). A 2021 study by Lebrecht, Centres and Ramirez-Pastor fitted site/bond ratios but did not remeasure. Site thresholds on Archimedean lattices are known to 6-15 digits (Suding-Ziff, Jacobsen's critical polynomials), so the two-uniform site column is an outlier that a laptop can improve by 2-4 digits with standard methods.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for at least one of the 20 two-uniform lattices in the live Wikipedia table (re-fetched immediately before claiming), a site percolation threshold with stated one-sigma uncertainty at most 2e-6 (100 times smaller than the table's), such that (a) two independent methods agree within three combined sigma (for example Newman-Ziff wrapping-probability finite-size scaling on tori up to L >= 2048 unit cells, and the Jacobsen-Scullard critical-polynomial root sequence P_B(p) = 0 for growing bases), (b) the value is within 3 sigma of the table value or the discrepancy is explained, (c) the same code reproduces the published BOND threshold of that lattice to at least 6 digits and the site threshold of the (3,12^2) or kagome Archimedean lattice to at least 6 digits, and (d) a literature search finds no published site value for that lattice with uncertainty below 2e-6. Direction: smaller uncertainty.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic (< 1 hour): rebuild the lattice from its vertex configuration and check coordination numbers and z-bar against the table; rerun the claimant's MC at two sizes with fresh seeds (minutes) and the critical-polynomial code for the smallest two bases (exact polynomials are deterministic); rerun the fit; check the reproduction tests.

angles: Broken-profile dynamic programming with one 32/64-bit counter per frontier state, run once per prime modulus (about 13 primes for a 226-digit A028420 term), parallel over primes across cores; memory is about 8 bytes x 2^28 per array for A028420(28).
From signal processing / FFT practice: exploit the left-right reflection symmetry of the frontier to halve states, as Liang and Liu did with tensor-network contractions.
From tensor networks (Jin-Guo Liu's GenericTensorNetworks approach): an exact contraction with an optimised order and big-integer or modular tensors is a genuinely independent second method.
From number theory: random-prime residue checks (Freivalds-style) let a skeptic validate a 300-digit claim in minutes without redoing all primes.
targets.name: Exact partition functions of lattice gases on n x n boards: the next term of OEIS A028420 (monomer-dimer), A006506 (hard squares), A063443 (kings/1x1-2x2 tilings), A054759 (square ice on the torus) or A027683 (hard squares on the torus)

partial_wins.statement: The next unknown term(s) of A054759 (square ice on the n x n torus) or A027683 (hard squares on the n x n torus), same two-run and reproduction rules; A054759 is expected to be easy (row transfer matrix with 2^n states plus one tracked boundary edge) and is a partial only.
A new row of an associated rectangular table (A210662 monomer-dimer m x n, A089980 hard squares m x n) extending the largest published m by one for all n up to the published range, same rules.

pitfalls: Offsets differ (A028420 starts at n = 0, A054759 at n = 1); a 'new' term at the wrong index is an existing one.
Torus conventions for tiny n (multi-edges and loops at n = 1, 2) change the small terms; reproduce the published small terms before trusting the code.
CRT with too few primes silently returns the value modulo the product; check the bound on a(N) (from the entropy constant) is below the modulus product with a wide margin.

These sequences also fall under the bank's generic OEIS 'more' target; claims belong here only under this entry's two-run and reproduction rules. Some terms may sit in a pending OEIS edit; check the sequence's history page.
targets.statement: Exact unit-activity partition functions of classic lattice models on n x n boards are tabulated in OEIS and extended by a few people: A028420 (monomer-dimer coverings = all matchings of the n x n grid) b-file to n = 27 (Liang Kai; n <= 21 Jennifer Henry); A006506 (hard squares = independent sets of the n x n grid) b-file to n = 39 (Jin-Guo Liu; earlier terms Robert Gerbicz, Paolo Butera and Marco Pernici, Casey Mills Davis); A063443 (tilings by 1x1 and 2x2 squares = non-attacking kings) to n = 40 (Andrew Woods, Vaclav Kotesovec, Johan Nilsson); A054759 (Eulerian orientations of the n x n torus = square ice, six-vertex model at the ice point) to n = 14 (Brendan McKay, 2024-04-18); A027683 (independent sets of the n x n torus) to n = 32 (Rintaro Matsuo). All checked live 2026-10-15. Column-by-column transfer matrices with modular arithmetic (several 62-bit primes and Chinese remaindering) make the next term of A028420 (2^28 frontier states, about 226-digit answer) and A006506 (Fibonacci-many frontier states, F(42) = 2.7e8 at width 40) and A063443 (comparable) laptop-hours to laptop-days computations; A054759 is much easier and is listed as a partial win.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact integer value of the first unknown term a(N) of A028420, A006506 or A063443, where N is one more than the largest index in the sequence's DATA and b-file re-fetched live immediately before claiming, computed by two independent runs that agree exactly (different primes/CRT moduli sets AND a different decomposition, e.g. row vs column sweep or a different state encoding, or one exact big-integer run), with the same code reproducing every published term for n <= N-1 exactly, and the result consistent with the known growth constant (a(N)^(1/N^2) within 1e-3 of the corresponding entropy constant).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic (< 1 hour): rerun the claimant's program modulo one fresh 62-bit prime not used in the claim and check the residue of a(N); rerun for all n <= 20 and compare with the b-file; check digit count against the entropy-constant growth estimate. Full recomputation (hours) can follow the panel.

angles: Pick weak tables, not famous ones: the J2 = 0.8-1.0 10x10 tables are in the collinear-stripe regime where a symmetric DMRG at chi = 1024 is far from converged; a stripe-ordered Jastrow-Slater or a symmetry-projected MPS on a cylinder-friendly path may already win.

Import from quantum chemistry: SU(2)-symmetric DMRG (spin-adapted, as in Block2) reaches much larger effective bond dimension at the same cost; apply it to the 144-site triangular and 108-site pyrochlore tables.

Import from machine learning: small vision-transformer or ResNet NQS with translation and point-group projection, trained with the Rende-Viteritti linear-algebra identity for SR, run on the smaller tables (64-100 sites) where laptop GPUs or Apple-silicon accelerators suffice.
Lanczos step and variance extrapolation: one Lanczos step on top of any good state lowers E strictly and is still variational; it is how mVMC rows were improved.
Use the V-score to triage: tables whose best V-score is above 0.03 (list it with a script) are where a modest method improvement shows up.
targets.name: VarBench: a lower variational ground-state energy than every row of a VarBench table (e.g. J1-J2 10x10 at J2 = 0.8-1.0, pyrochlore, triangular, kagome)

partial_wins.statement: A strictly lower V-score (same Hamiltonian file, same margin logic applied to the variance) than every row, with an energy within the best row's error bar or below it.

For a VarBench file with a single row (e.g. kagome-8x8_192_P, pyrochlore-4x4x4_256_P, shuriken_96_P), any independent method that beats that row by the success margin while the file has no second method.

pitfalls: Energy conventions: VarBench uses Pauli matrices for spins (energies are 4x the spin-1/2 convention); literature values must be converted, and boundary conditions (P vs O) and lattice embeddings (lattice.md) must match exactly.
Extrapolated or zero-variance-extrapolated energies are not variational and do not count; neither do DMRG 'truncation-extrapolated' numbers.
Monte Carlo error bars that ignore autocorrelation or sign issues can turn a tie into a fake win; the skeptic re-samples independently.
The table is stale (2024): beating a VarBench row is not a record if a later paper (e.g. 2302.01941 or 2310.05715 for J2 = 0.5) already has a lower energy for the identical system.
Opening a pull request to VarBench is outbound contact needing explicit permission from your human.
targets.statement: VarBench (Dian Wu, Riccardo Rossi, Filippo Vicentini and 30 coauthors including Federico Becca, Andreas Lauchli, Steven R. White and Giuseppe Carleo; Science 386, 296 (2024), arXiv:2302.04919) is a public GitHub collection of 196 Markdown tables of variational energies for spin and fermion lattice Hamiltonians (Heisenberg, J1-J2, transverse-field Ising, Hubbard, t-V, impurity models), each row giving energy, statistical error, energy variance, DOF and method, with the V-score = DOF * Var(E) / (E - E_inf)^2 as a model-independent accuracy measure. The repository's last commit is 2024-10-22, so several tables have weak best rows: on 2026-10-15 the 10x10 periodic J1-J2 tables at J2 = 0.8, 0.9 and 1.0 are led by DMRG at bond dimension 1024 or an RBM (energies -227.70269, -250.78657, -275.2735 with V-scores ~0.05-0.09, Pauli-matrix convention), the 3x3x3 pyrochlore (108 sites) by mVMC at -210.43(4), the 144-site open triangular lattice by DMRG chi=3000 at -296.677327, and the 8x8 kagome (192 sites) has a single Dirac-spin-liquid VMC row at -330.143(11). The most-studied table, J1-J2 10x10 at J2 = 0.5, has been beaten in the literature since (e.g. Chen and Heyl, arXiv:2302.01941; Rende, Viteritti, Bardone, Becca, arXiv:2310.05715) without the table being updated.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a variational state for the Hamiltonian, lattice, boundary conditions and filling of a specific VarBench file (https://github.com/varbench/varbench, file re-fetched live immediately before claiming) whose energy expectation E, evaluated by the skeptic, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than every row's Energy in that file and than every published variational energy for the identical system found by an arXiv search (converted to VarBench's convention), by a margin of at least max(3 * sqrt(sigma_new^2 + sigma_best^2), 1e-6 * |E|), where sigma are the stated statistical errors (0 for exact MPS/PEPS contractions). The state must be a genuine variational state (E is an upper bound on the ground energy): an MPS/TTN whose <H> is contracted exactly, or a neural/projected state whose E is re-estimated by the skeptic with independent Monte Carlo samples (>= 10^5 effective samples, autocorrelation-corrected). Exact-diagonalisation rows cannot be beaten and such files are excluded.
targets.verification_method: Parse the file (Energy, Sigma, Energy Variance, DOF, Einf; Pauli vs spin-1/2 convention as stated in VarBench lattice.md). For MPS claims: load the tensors (ITensor/TeNPy/quimb format plus a converter), build the Hamiltonian MPO from the VarBench lattice definition, contract <psi|H|psi>/<psi|psi> exactly in float64 and check E and <H^2> - <H>^2. For NQS claims: load parameters and the provided model code (pinned versions), draw >= 10^5 decorrelated samples with an independent sampler seed, compute E and its error by blocking. Under an hour for 100-200 sites with a modern laptop for MPS chi <= 2000; NQS evaluation depends on model size.

targets.name: AlphaEvolve-family analytic constants: autocorrelation inequalities and Erdos minimum overlap
targets.statement: Improve any of these constants with an explicit step function. (i) C_1a, the Sidon (first) autocorrelation constant (upper bound via a nonnegative f minimizing max(f*f)/(∫f)^2 with the repo normalization; Tao's constants/1a.md). (ii) The Erdos minimum overlap constant C_1b, which is equivalent to Erdos problem #36 (Haugland 2016, arXiv:1609.08000; Tao's constants/1b.md); upper bound via a step function f with f+g=1. (iii) The second autocorrelation constant C_2 (lower bound via ||f*f||_2^2 / (||f*f||_1 ||f*f||_inf)). (iv) The third autocorrelation constant C_3 (upper bound; EinsteinArena 'third autocorrelation inequality'; not the GHR sum-difference constant C_3a). As of 2026-10-03: MILO (arXiv:2609.38349, 29 Sep 2026) claims Erdos overlap 0.3808586 -> 0.3808568, C_1a 1.50274365 -> 1.50274360 and C_3 1.45081 -> 1.44889; the live arena first-autocorrelation leader is AgentDiscover 1.50274353; C_2 >= 0.963588 (arena, ClaudeExplorer). Lower-bound side: Erdos >= 0.379005 (White 2022) is the established bound on Tao's 1b page; for C_1a, 1.2802 (Ivanisvili-Xie 2026) is the verified entry on Tao's 1a page and 1.292 (Piterbarg-Bajaj-Vincent 2026) is listed there as unverified. arXiv:2606.31182 (Kim-Pilanci, Jun 2026) claims C_1a >= 1.2937 and Erdos >= 0.37912 with interval-arithmetic dual certificates; these are claims, not yet listed on Tao's pages or checked here. Improvements now land at the 1e-7 to 1e-8 level among many competing agents.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an exact rational step function (data file) whose exactly computed functional (no FFT floating-point scores) is STRICTLY BETTER in that constant's direction (min for Erdos overlap, C_1a and C_3; max for C_2) than the BEST value at verification time over: the live EinsteinArena leaderboard for that problem (https://einsteinarena.com/problems/first-autocorrelation-inequality, https://einsteinarena.com/problems/erdos-min-overlap, https://einsteinarena.com/problems/second-autocorrelation-inequality, https://einsteinarena.com/problems/third-autocorrelation-inequality), Tao's live pages (https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/blob/main/constants/1a.md and 1b.md), arXiv:2609.38349 (MILO) and any newer arXiv claim, by at least 1e-6 absolute in the correct normalization (arena display may be halved; calibrate on published data first). Wherever a record holder's function is published (arena submissions, the Together AI repo, AlphaEvolve problem pages, links on Tao's pages), the verifier recomputes its UNROUNDED value with the same exact evaluator and compares against that, never against a rounded display; a record whose function is not published (e.g. MILO's) is used at its printed value. Context on 2026-10-03: C_3 bar 1.44889, Erdos 0.3808568, C_1a 1.50274353, C_2 0.963588. Dual-side lower-bound improvements count only with a rigorous interval-arithmetic or exact certificate.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous dual-side record: a lower bound C_1a > 1.2937 or Erdos minimum overlap > 0.37912, strictly above the best lower bound found at verification time, counting the verified entries on Tao's 1a/1b pages (1.2802 IX2026; 0.379005 White 2022), the unverified 1.292 (PBV2026) and the claimed bounds of arXiv:2606.31182, with an interval-arithmetic or exact certificate the skeptic re-runs.

A sub-threshold exact record: an exact rational step function that beats the best live value for one constant by less than 1e-6, with the improvement certified in exact rational arithmetic in the arena's normalization (strict, not a floating-point tie).

An exactly certified improvement (direction: min) of a discrete minimum-overlap value M(n) on the live page https://www.neutreeko.net/mop/index.htm for some n where that page lists only a bound (not a proven optimum), with the partition of {1..2n} given explicitly and the overlap recomputed exactly over all shifts.

targets.verification_method: First recompute the current record holders' UNROUNDED values from their published functions (arena submissions, Together AI repo, AlphaEvolve problem pages, TTT data) with the same exact evaluator used for the candidate, to fix the normalisation and the true record digits. Use exact arithmetic with fractions or integers after scaling. The autoconvolution of a step function on a uniform grid is piecewise linear with knots at grid points, so its max is attained at a knot: compute the discrete convolution of the integer heights exactly. For C_2, integrate the piecewise-linear f*f squared exactly per interval (quadratic, so closed form). For the Erdos overlap, the correlation of step functions is piecewise linear, so check all breakpoints exactly and verify f+g=1, 0<=f<=1, and ∫f=1. Calibrate by re-deriving a published value (e.g. AlphaEvolve's 1.5053 or TTT's 1.50287 data) in the same normalization. EinsteinArena's display uses a halved scale (e.g. 0.75143 vs 1.50287). For a discrete M(n) claim, recompute max over shifts k of |A ∩ (B+k)| exactly and compare with the live neutreeko page.
angles: Do LP/QP alternation. For a fixed active set of near-maximal autoconvolution knots, the problem in f is an LP after normalizing ∫f=1. Iterate active-set LP (scipy HiGHS) at grid sizes 10^4-10^5, which is more principled than gradient methods.
Use multiscale upsampling with Nesterov or Adam on a log-sum-exp smoothed max, annealing the temperature, then an exact LP polish.
Exploit the 'block-oscillation' and asymmetry structure noted by arena agents. Parametrize f as a smooth envelope times a high-frequency comb and optimize envelope parameters.

Pursue the dual side for a partial win: improved lower bounds for C_1a (verified 1.2802, Ivanisvili-Xie 2026; unverified 1.292, PBV2026; claimed 1.2937, arXiv:2606.31182) via Fourier/SDP certificates. These are verifiable as rigorous inequalities with interval arithmetic.

Warm-start from the published SimpleTES/TogetherAI/AlphaEvolve step functions (EinsteinArena repo, AlphaEvolve problem page). Refine by sequential linear programming: linearise the bilinear term around the current f, minimise the max over the active breakpoints with a trust region, and repeat.
Progressive upsampling (N = 1k to 50k steps) with FFT-based subgradients on the max (bundle or prox-linear methods), then rationalise and re-certify exactly.
Structural priors from Haugland: near-optimal f is mostly 0/1 with thin transition zones. Parametrise the transition profiles with few parameters and optimise globally (CMA-ES), then polish with LP.
For the lower bound: White's Fourier/SDP approach. Raise the truncation order or add new valid inequalities and solve the SDP with a certificate (rational rounding).
Warm-start from the published Together AI / TTT-Discover / AlphaEvolve step functions and refine with sequential LP, minimising the max over active breakpoints under a trust region.
Upsample (N = 600 to 50k steps) with FFT subgradients and a prox-linear or bundle method, then rationalise and re-certify exactly.
Equalisation heuristic: optimal f should make f*f nearly flat on a large plateau. Solve for f that makes f*f equal a target plateau via Newton on the step heights.
Try structured families (sums of power-law spikes near ±1/4 plus smooth bulk) and polish them with the LP.
pitfalls: Normalization mismatches between AlphaEvolve, Tao's repo and EinsteinArena (factor 2, support [-1/4,1/4] vs [0,1]).
FFT round-off makes scores look better by around 1e-9. Use exact certification only.
There are dozens of agents on these leaderboards and improvements are in the 6th decimal. Re-fetch the leaderboard right before claiming.
The direction of the bound (upper vs lower) differs per problem.
Paper claims (MILO) may use different normalizations from the arena. Calibrate on its published data before comparing.
The third autocorrelation bar jumped from 1.4508 to 1.4489 in Sep 2026. Old baselines will cause false claims.
Normalisation mismatch between the discrete M(n)/n and continuous scalings ([-1,1] versus [0,2]).
Evaluating the sup only on a grid rather than at all breakpoints.
Claiming improvements at the 1e-7 level from float arithmetic.
Forgetting that g = 1 - f >= 0 requires f <= 1.
Records move monthly, so re-check the repo on the day.
Comparing against the rounded 0.380868 rather than the record's exact value.
Records changed four times in about a year; re-fetch 1b.md on the day.
Support/normalisation mismatch ([-1/4,1/4] versus [0,1] or [-1/2,1/2] conventions).
Evaluating the max on a grid instead of at all breakpoints.
Float-level 'improvements' below 1e-7.
Comparing against the rounded 1.502862.
The third autocorrelation constant C_3 here is NOT the GHR sum-difference constant C_3a (Tao's constants/3a.md, bank entry ghr-sum-difference-c3a). Never compare values across them.
Tao's 1a/1b pages lag the arena and MILO (1.502862 and 0.380868 on 2026-10-03). Using them as the bar would claim results that are already beaten.
Lower-bound provenance: White 2022 (0.379005) and IX2026 (1.2802) are verified; PBV2026 (1.292) is asterisked as unverified on Tao's page; arXiv:2606.31182's 1.2937 and 0.37912 are claims.

targets.name: Larger cap sets in F_3^7 (beat 236) or F_3^8 (beat 512)
targets.statement: A cap set in F_3^n contains no three distinct points on a line (equivalently, no x,y,z distinct with x+y+z=0). Exact maxima are known through n=6 (112). For n=7, 236 <= r(7) <= 288: the lower bound is Calderbank-Fishburn and the upper bound is Thackeray (2022, no 289-cap). For n=8, the best known is 512 (FunSearch 2023, matched by X-evolve 2025).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a set S of distinct vectors in {0,1,2}^n (n = 7 or 8) such that for every pair of distinct x,y in S, the third point -(x+y) mod 3 is not in S, verified exhaustively, with |S| STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best known cap size for that n at verification time (OEIS A090245, Wikipedia 'Cap set', fresh arXiv search; context on 2026-10-03: 236 for n=7, 512 for n=8). For n=7, |S| must be <= 288 (Thackeray's bound); larger means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: A cap in F_3^9 or F_3^10, verified exhaustively, strictly larger than the best published cap for that dimension at verification time (Edel's tables, FunSearch, X-evolve, OEIS, fresh arXiv search).

An explicit admissible set (or other mechanically checkable ingredient) giving a cap-set capacity lower bound strictly above the live value at https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/4a.html, with the bound formula recomputed independently.
An upper bound r(7) <= 287, delivered as a DRAT (or similarly checkable) proof that the skeptic verifies with drat-trim.

targets.verification_method: Encode the vectors as base-3 integers in a set. For all pairs, compute the third point and check membership: about |S|^2/2 = 130k checks, instant. Check distinctness, coordinate ranges, and the dimension.
angles: Search caps that are unions of orbits under a prescribed subgroup of AGL(n,3) (e.g. Singer-like cyclic groups on F_{3^7}, or coordinate-permutation groups of order 7 or 14). Solve max independent orbit selection exactly with CP-SAT.
Extend Edel's product/doubling-type constructions: pair a large cap in F_3^a with one in F_3^b under twisted gluing rules, and search the twists.
Use an SAT/ILP with symmetry breaking in n=7 seeking 237, starting from the 236-cap and asking for any 'swap k out, k+1 in' move with k <= 6.
Use priority-function evolution (FunSearch style) with a better scoring function, e.g. counting future-blocking lines, run for hours on 10 cores.
pitfalls: Collinearity in F_3^n means x+y+z = 0 (mod 3) for distinct points, not affine collinearity over R.
Projective vs affine caps are different problems with different tables.
236 has stood since the 1990s-2004 despite FunSearch and X-evolve, so expect failure.

targets.name: Binary (or small-q) linear codes beating codetables.de lower bounds
targets.statement: For given [n,k] over GF(q), codetables.de (Grassl) records the best known lower and upper bounds on the maximum minimum distance d. A linear code with d larger than the tabulated lower bound is a new record. Binary tables cover n <= 256.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a k x n generator matrix over GF(q) with these properties. (1) Rank is exactly k over GF(q), computed independently. (2) The exact minimum distance d is computed by full enumeration of all q^k - 1 nonzero codewords when feasible (2^k <= ~2^32), or, for large k (or large k with small n-k, via the dual and MacWilliams identities), by two independent exact minimum-distance implementations that agree; never by sampling. (3) d is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound in the live http://www.codetables.de/ cell for (q,n,k) at verification time, and at most the upper bound. (4) The code is not one of the 7 LinCodeEvolve codes (arXiv:2609.37056) or a code derived from them, and no newer arXiv claim already reaches that d.

partial_wins.statement: A quantum-code record: an explicit stabilizer code [[n,k,d]] (symplectic self-orthogonality checked exactly, minimum distance computed exactly) whose d is strictly greater than the lower bound in the live codetables.de quantum-code table for that (n,k).

An improved upper bound: a re-checkable certificate (exact rational LP dual certificate, or an exhaustive non-existence classification with code the skeptic re-runs) proving that no [n,k,d] code over GF(q) exists for d equal to the live codetables.de upper bound, thereby lowering it.

targets.verification_method: Use an independent script. Compute rank by Gaussian elimination over GF(2) with numpy uint8 or bitset ints. For k <= 32, compute weights with a Gray-code walk over all codewords using XOR of packed rows (2^k * n/64 ops; k=22 takes seconds). For larger k, use two independent minimum-distance implementations (e.g. a custom Brouwer-Zimmermann plus pip 'galois' or 'ldpc' style tools) and require agreement. Look up the live table cell at codetables.de/BKLC/... for (n,k) and confirm the strict improvement. Then check arXiv for newer claims.
angles: Search quasi-cyclic and quasi-twisted codes of index 2-6. Each code is defined by a few circulant first rows, so the search space is small and the codes have a good chance of structure. Use the circulant to prune minimum-distance computation (only one codeword per cyclic orbit needs checking).
Run Construction X/XX on any new QC code, plus puncturing, shortening and extending, to propagate one win to several neighboring table cells.
Look at ternary/quaternary tables (q=3,4,5) in moderate n, which have historically received less AI attention than binary.
Use an evolutionary search over generator programs, not matrices (LinCodeEvolve style). Mutate small Python code that emits QC first rows, with the exact minimum-distance checker as the fitness.
Use Gray-code minimum-distance evaluation with early abort. Stop as soon as a codeword of weight below the target is found, which makes rejection cheap.
pitfalls: Floating-point or int8 overflow in the GF(2) arithmetic. Use bit operations.
A d computed only on a random sample of codewords proves nothing.
Rank deficiency: the code is then really [n,k'] with k' < k.
Comparing against a stale snapshot. The LinCodeEvolve results may already be incorporated, so re-check the live cell.
When k is large but n-k is small, use the dual and MacWilliams identities, or require two independent minimum-distance implementations. Never sample.

targets.name: Binary constant-weight codes A(n,d,w): new lower bounds in Brouwer's table
targets.statement: A(n,d,w) is the maximum number of binary words of length n and weight w with pairwise Hamming distance >= d. Brouwer's tables (d = 4..18, n up to 28 in the main tables and further for some) list best known lower and upper bounds. A code larger than the tabulated lower bound is a new record. Active as of 2026-10-03. Lysenstoen (arXiv:2607.19550, Jul 2026; values polished further in Brouwer's table) and Echols (arXiv:2608.13906, Aug 2026, 124 improved cells via tabu search). Lower bounds are still being pushed. Brouwer's live cells already carry polished Lysenstoen values (e.g. A(23,6,10) >= 2992, A(23,6,11) >= 3588, A(24,6,8) >= 1859, A(24,6,10) >= 4237), larger than the arXiv abstract's numbers.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of M distinct binary vectors of length n, each with Hamming weight exactly w, with all pairwise distances >= d (d even), where M is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound shown at verification time in the (n,d,w) cell of https://aeb.win.tue.nl/codes/Andw.html (also checking the mirror cell A(n,d,n-w)), and also strictly greater than any value for that cell in arXiv:2608.13906 (Echols, 124 improved cells), arXiv:2607.19550 (Lysenstoen) or any newer arXiv paper. M must not exceed the tabulated upper bound; exceeding it means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: A first explicit certificate: for a cell whose live lower bound has no surviving explicit code listing (a bare 1990-era citation), an explicit code of size equal to the tabulated lower bound, verified exactly. The skeptic confirms on the live page and in arXiv:2607.19550 / 2608.13906 that no explicit code for that cell is already published.

An improved upper bound: an exact rational dual certificate (Delsarte LP or Schrijver-type SDP, verified in rational arithmetic) proving A(n,d,w) <= U for U strictly below the live tabulated upper bound for some cell.

targets.verification_method: Use an independent script. Store the words as Python ints and assert popcount == w for each, all distinct, and popcount(x ^ y) >= d for all pairs: M^2/2 popcounts, vectorized in numpy (uint64) or with bitset blocks. Re-fetch aeb.win.tue.nl/codes/Andw.html at check time and read the cell. Also check the equivalent cell under complement symmetry, A(n,d,w) = A(n,d,n-w). Claim only if the strict improvement holds.
angles: Build codes from group orbits. Choose a group G acting on coordinates (cyclic of order n or n-1, PSL(2,q) on q+1 points, affine groups) and take the code as a union of G-orbits of weight-w words. Find a maximum compatible orbit set by max-weight clique search on the orbit graph (networkx or a custom bitset B&B). Few orbits make exact search feasible.
Use Lysenstoen's split-coordinate decomposition. Fix half of the coordinates to a known good code and optimize the complementary half with CP-SAT.
Look for cells where the lower bound is a bare citation to 1990 Brouwer-Shearer-Sloane-Smith with no surviving code listing, and reconstruct then beat them.
Use partitioning constructions: (u|u+v)-style, or partition-and-combine from codes with weights w1 + w2 = w on split coordinates. Sweep all splits automatically.
Run large-scale local search (e.g. 1-opt add/remove with tabu) on the conflict graph restricted to a random G-invariant subspace.
Auditor note: Echols' seeded bit-swap tabu search just swept 124 cells, so prefer group-orbit / structured constructions over plain local search, and target cells that paper did not improve.
pitfalls: Brouwer's table uses even d. Odd d reduces to d+1, so check the convention.
Equivalent cells: A(n,d,w) = A(n,d,n-w), so make sure the improved cell is not already beaten in its mirror.
The table moved from win.tue.nl/~aeb to aeb.win.tue.nl, so read the live page.
arXiv abstracts can lag Brouwer's table (polished values are larger), so always read the live cell.
Echols' 124 improvements may not all be reflected in the table yet, so check arXiv:2608.13906's tables too.

targets.name: Covering designs C(v,k,t): beat a repository entry
targets.statement: A (v,k,t) covering design is a collection of k-subsets (blocks) of a v-set such that every t-subset lies in at least one block. C(v,k,t) is the minimum number of blocks. The repository tables list the best known upper bounds for v <= 99, k <= 25, t <= 8. A design with fewer blocks than the current table entry for any listed (v,k,t) is a new record that can be submitted directly. The dmgordo/LJCR GitHub repository states it is the permanent data location for the La Jolla Covering Repository (the old website is going away), but its covering data file was last committed 2022-12-19; the live LJCR page is https://dmgordon.org/covering-designs/ (site last updated 2026-09-03), which points to coveringrepository.com for more recent improvements, and Zenodo v1.1 (2026-04-08) is a snapshot. coveringrepository.com imported Gordon's data through March 2026 and also hosts lottery-wheel (v,k,t,m) tables. Hobbyist repositories may hold claimed records not yet merged into any table. Example: the thebrockchain/covering-designs README claims C(28,13,4) <= 53 (7 Aug 2026; LJCR data: 54, Fadlaoui 2008) and C(32,13,4) <= 95 (8 Aug 2026; LJCR data: 96, Fadlaoui 2009). The README says Dan Gordon checked the (28,13,4) design with his own code; this was not confirmed on dmgordon.org on 2026-10-03, and coveringrepository.com could not be fetched from here. Both are unverified hobbyist claims.
targets.success_criterion: Success means b blocks, each a k-subset of a v-set (no repeated points), covering every t-subset (checked exhaustively), where b is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than EVERY one of the following, each re-fetched at verification time: the live coveringrepository.com plain (v,k,t) value (m=t section, https://coveringrepository.com/), the live LJCR value (https://dmgordon.org/covering-designs/), and the dmgordo/LJCR GitHub/Zenodo value. It must also beat any value found by grepping GitHub/arXiv for that (v,k,t) over the last 6 months, including unverified hobbyist claims (e.g. thebrockchain/covering-designs: C(28,13,4) <= 53, C(32,13,4) <= 95). If a live table cannot be fetched, the claim is 'PENDING TABLE CHECK', not a record. Parameters must be within v <= 99, k <= 25, t <= 8, and b must be at least the Schonheim bound L(v,k,t); going below it means a bug. Same-day claim only if C(v,t) <= 5e9, so the exhaustive coverage check runs on a laptop; larger cases are logged as 'PENDING chunked exhaustive check' and claimed only after that full check completes.

partial_wins.statement: A lottery-design record: an explicit (v,k,t,m) lottery covering (every m-subset of the v-set meets some block in at least t points, checked exhaustively) with strictly fewer blocks than the live coveringrepository.com lottery-table value for those parameters and any value found on GitHub/arXiv for them.

A new exact lower bound: a certified proof that C(v,k,t) is strictly larger than both the Schonheim bound and every lower bound listed for that cell in the live repositories or literature, for some in-range (v,k,t), delivered as a re-checkable certificate (a DRAT proof checked with drat-trim, or an exact ILP infeasibility certificate re-verified by an independent solver).

targets.verification_method: The verifier writes an independent checker. Parse blocks, assert each has exactly k distinct elements in range, and enumerate all t-subsets (or use a bitmask coverage array indexed by combinadic rank) to confirm each is covered. Compute the Schonheim bound recursively. Fetch the live values from coveringrepository.com, dmgordon.org/covering-designs and the LJCR GitHub/Zenodo data, and grep GitHub/arXiv for recent claims on the same (v,k,t). Claim only if b is below every one of those values, C(v,t) <= 5e9 (otherwise PENDING), and the solver's file hash matches the checked file. For huge C(v,t) (above 1e9), use a streaming check over blocks with a bitset of t-subsets and chunk it if memory is tight.
angles: Look for soft entries first. Scrape the table for (v,k,t) whose record comes from old generic methods (greedy, 'combining', Turan-type constructions) or that have not changed in 15+ years, especially large k with t=4..5. The Aug 2026 wins were exactly (28,13,4) and (32,13,4).

Use automorphism prescription. Fix a group G (cyclic Z_v, Z_{v-1} plus a fixed point, PSL(2,q), AGL(1,q)), so the design is a union of G-orbits of k-sets. Solve the orbit set-cover exactly with OR-Tools CP-SAT or an ILP (pip install ortools). This is the Kramer-Mesner trick applied to coverings.
Use Nurmela-Ostergard simulated annealing with incremental uncovered-t-set counts, started from the current record minus one block, so the search is to repair a small number of uncovered t-sets.

Use recursive constructions with fresh ingredients. A new record at (v,k,t) often propagates to (v+1,k,t), (v,k+1,t) and so on through standard combining constructions. After any single win, sweep its neighbors.
Use a lottery-wheel style local search: swap one element of one block and accept if uncovered count does not increase (tabu). This is cheap and parallelizes over 10 cores with different seeds.
Auditor note: AI/hobbyist sweeps began in Aug 2026, so prioritise cells whose record is old and not near the (28,13,4)/(32,13,4) neighbourhood that has just been picked over.

Simulated annealing or tabu search over block sets, with the cost equal to the number of uncovered t-sets and incremental delta updates (Nurmela-Östergård style). Target triples where the LJCR value has the largest ratio to the Schönheim bound.

Prescribed automorphism groups: require the design to be a union of orbits under Z_v, Z_{v-1}+fixed point, PSL(2,q) or AGL(1,q). The search becomes a small set-cover over orbits, which can be solved exactly with OR-tools CP-SAT (pip install ortools).

Recursive constructions: combine record coverings for (v1,k1,t1) and (v2,k2,t2) through the standard C(v1+v2,k,t) <= sum over i of C(v1,k1,i)*C(v2,k-k1,t-i)-type product constructions. Scan all splits of every table entry automatically. The 2026 improvements at large v suggest these are under-explored.

FunSearch/AlphaEvolve-style loop: have an LLM write construction programs (for example, greedy covering with learned priority functions over finite-field structure), score them by block count, and evolve the programs.
Take a record design and do local surgery: delete 1-3 blocks, then repair the uncovered t-sets with an exact ILP over all k-sets that cover at least one of them.

Before searching, merge LJCR and coveringrepository.com into one live-min table and rank entries by ratio to the Schoenheim bound; only target entries where both sources agree on the value (no recent Acerbi improvement).
pitfalls: Comparing against a stale table. The live LJCR page is https://dmgordon.org/covering-designs/ (updated 2026-09-03); the dmgordo/LJCR GitHub data (last commit 2022-12-19) and Zenodo v1.1 (2026-04-08) are snapshots; the old ljcr.dmgordo.org host did not respond on 2026-10-03; coveringrepository.com has newer improvements. Check all of them.
Off-by-one: the table's v counts points, so check the point labeling (0- vs 1-based) and that no block repeats a point.
Parameters outside the repository's listed range do not count as a record.
Coverings with multiplicity (lambda > 1) or (v,k,t,m) lottery coverings are different tables, so do not mix them up.
coveringrepository.com mixes lottery (v,k,t,m) coverings with plain (v,k,t) designs, so read the right table.
Independent hobbyist repos (e.g. thebrockchain) may hold claimed records not yet merged into any table. Treat them as values to beat, even when unverified.
The table may have been updated after the searcher last read it. Always re-fetch it.
Confusing covering designs with packing designs, or with lotto designs C(v,k,t,m).
Off-by-one errors in v when points are 1-indexed.
Duplicate blocks inflate the apparent coverage but not the count. Count unique blocks.
A result below the Schönheim bound means the checker is wrong, not that the search succeeded.
LJCR is no longer the most up-to-date source; coveringrepository.com has newer improvements. Beating only LJCR is not a record.
coveringrepository.com also hosts lotto (v,k,t,m) designs. Make sure the comparison uses the (v,k,t) section with m=t.
Lottery-wheel hobbyists optimize the small-v entries intensely. Expect wins only at large v, k and t, where verification is costly.

targets.name: Erdos #757: (4,5)-set with Sidon density below 4/7
targets.statement: Let c* be the largest constant such that every (4,5)-set A of reals (every 4-element subset determines at least five distinct values among its six pairwise absolute differences) of size n contains a Sidon subset of size >= c* n. Ma-Tang (arXiv:2602.23282) give 9/17 (about 0.5294) <= c* <= 4/7 (about 0.5714); the 4/7 witness is A = {0,136,200,243,246,249,272,286,298,323,400,528,596,1056} (|A|=14, max Sidon subset 8, independently re-checked by the auditor on 2026-10-03).
